name: ACH — Maker-Checker Self-Approval (Segregation-of-Duties Violation)
description:
Attacker objective
Bypass dual-control (segregation of duties) by having the same person both request (maker) and approve (checker) a privileged change such as a role assignment or user creation — insider fraud / privilege escalation.

Attack logic
A maker-checker workflow requires two distinct identities. A record where the maker and the checker are the same principal is a segregation-of-duties violation, whether from a control misconfiguration or deliberate fraud.

Why this detection works
The application audit records both the maker and the checker identity on each change, so comparing them directly surfaces self-approval with no baseline required.

False positives
None expected under a correctly configured SoD control; a legitimate emergency self-approval would still warrant review.

Tuning
None required; investigate every hit.

Required telemetry
ACH application audit (apps-*, type=ACHAPP): USERNAME_MAKER, USERNAME_CHECKER, ACTION_TASK, USERNAME_UPDATED.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. The same user made and approved a role/user change — a control failure or deliberate fraud.
2. Review ACTION_TASK and USERNAME_UPDATED (who was affected).
3. Escalate to the fraud/risk function.
false_positives: None expected under a correctly configured SoD control; a legitimate emergency self-approval would still warrant review.
query: FROM apps-* METADATA _id, _index, _version | WHERE type == "ACHAPP" AND USERNAME_MAKER IS NOT NULL AND USERNAME_CHECKER IS NOT NULL AND USERNAME_MAKER == USERNAME_CHECKER | KEEP @timestamp, ACTION_TASK, USERNAME_MAKER, USERNAME_CHECKER, USERNAME_UPDATED

name: ACH — Role or User Change Submitted by an Unexpected Maker
description:
Attacker objective
Escalate privilege or plant an accomplice account in the ACH payment system by submitting a role assignment, role revocation, or user addition as an unauthorized maker.

Attack logic
ACH privilege changes follow a maker-checker workflow performed by a small, fixed set of authorized makers. A change submitted by a maker never seen before is outside the sanctioned administration set and may be a compromised account or a control bypass.

Why this detection works
A new-terms model over the maker identity auto-baselines the authorized makers and fires only when a genuinely new maker submits an ACH privilege change.

False positives
Onboarding of a new authorized ACH administrator.

Tuning
Verify and allowlist new authorized makers; pair with the maker-checker self-approval detection; review the role/user change and the checker.

Required telemetry
ACH application audit (apps-*, type=ACHAPP): USERNAME_MAKER, USERNAME_CHECKER, ACTION_TASK, USERNAME_UPDATED.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. USERNAME_MAKER = the submitting operator; ACTION_TASK/USERNAME_UPDATED show the change and target.
2. Confirm the maker is an authorized ACH administrator; an unexpected maker on the payment system is high-risk — involve fraud/risk.
3. Check whether the same change was self-approved (maker == checker).
false_positives: Onboarding of a new authorized ACH administrator.
query: type:"ACHAPP" and USERNAME_MAKER:*

name: ECC — Mass User/Role/Group Administration by One Operator
description:
Attacker objective
Manipulate access at scale in the ECC banking application — mass-modifying users, deleting roles, or removing groups — as a compromised or rogue operator, to escalate privilege or disrupt access.

Attack logic
ECC records every user/role/group administration action with the operator identity. A single operator performing an unusually high volume of these changes in a short window indicates mass privilege manipulation rather than routine day-to-day administration.

Why this detection works
Aggregating ECC administration actions per operator over a short window separates a mass-change burst from the steady, low per-operator rate of normal administration.

False positives
A legitimate bulk role/reorganisation or onboarding/offboarding batch performed by an authorized operator.

Tuning
Set the per-operator burst threshold above the routine administration rate; allowlist sanctioned bulk-change windows; review the operations and affected users.

Required telemetry
ECC application audit (apps-*, type=ECC_USR_AUDIT): USRADT_LOGIN_NAME (operator), USRADT_OPERATION/USRADT_ACTION, USR_LOGIN_NAME (target), USRADT_WS.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. operator = the ECC admin identity; review the operations (user/role/group changes) and the affected users.
2. Confirm whether a sanctioned bulk change was scheduled; if not, treat as a compromised/rogue operator and disable the account pending review.
3. Correlate the operator's workstation (USRADT_WS) and login with endpoint/AD activity.
false_positives: A legitimate bulk role/reorganisation or onboarding/offboarding batch performed by an authorized operator.
query:
FROM apps-*, -apps-*-2025 METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE type == "ECC_USR_AUDIT" AND USRADT_LOGIN_NAME IS NOT NULL
| EVAL operator = MV_FIRST(SPLIT(USRADT_LOGIN_NAME, "@"))
| STATS changes = COUNT(), operations = VALUES(USRADT_OPERATION), targets = VALUES(USR_LOGIN_NAME) BY operator
| WHERE changes >= 30

name: AD – Account Created / Enabled
description: AD – Account Created / Enabled

name: AD — AS-REP Roasting: TGT Requested for a Pre-Auth-Disabled Account
description:
Attacker objective
Obtain an AS-REP for an account that does not require Kerberos pre-authentication, then crack its password offline (AS-REP Roasting).

Attack logic
When 'do not require Kerberos pre-authentication' is set on an account, a Domain Controller returns an AS-REP encrypted with the account's password to any requester. In a hardened domain pre-authentication is enforced, so a pre-auth-disabled TGT request is anomalous.

Why this detection works
The AS-REQ event (4768) records the pre-authentication type; a value indicating no pre-authentication surfaces roastable requests directly.

False positives
A legacy application account that genuinely requires pre-authentication disabled.

Tuning
Allowlist verified legacy accounts; better, re-enable pre-authentication on them. Investigate any new occurrence.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4768 (PreAuthType).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. TargetUserName is the roastable account. Confirm whether pre-authentication was disabled deliberately.
2. Re-enable pre-authentication and reset the account password (long/complex); hunt for offline cracking.
false_positives: A legacy application account that genuinely requires pre-authentication disabled.
query: event.code:"4768" and winlog.event_data.PreAuthType:"0"

name: AD — DCSync: Directory Replication by an Unexpected Principal
description:
Attacker objective
Replicate the directory (DCSync) to pull password hashes for any account — including krbtgt — without touching a Domain Controller's disk.

Attack logic
The Directory Replication Service exposes the DS-Replication-Get-Changes(-All) control-access rights. Only Domain Controllers and sanctioned directory-sync services should exercise them; any other principal doing so is running DCSync (e.g. via Mimikatz).

Why this detection works
Object-access auditing (4662) records the replication access-control GUIDs and the requesting principal. Excluding Domain Controller computer accounts and sanctioned sync/identity services leaves only anomalous replication.

False positives
A directory-sync or identity-management service not yet in the exclusion, or a new Domain Controller. Human/interactive accounts triggering replication are almost never legitimate.

Tuning
Allowlist verified replication service accounts (identity sync, IGA tooling) after confirmation; investigate every human account that replicates.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4662 with Properties containing the replication GUIDs (1131f6aa / 1131f6ad) and AccessMask 0x100. Requires directory-object replication-property SACL auditing (already enabled here).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName is the replicating principal; a non-DC, non-service account performing GetChanges is DCSync.
2. If confirmed, treat the domain as compromised: reset all privileged accounts and rotate KRBTGT twice.
3. Correlate with the host the principal logged on from and any preceding privilege escalation.
false_positives: A directory-sync or identity-management service not yet in the exclusion, or a new Domain Controller. Human/interactive accounts triggering replication are almost never legitimate.
query: event.code:"4662" and winlog.event_data.AccessMask:"0x100" and (winlog.event_data.Properties:*1131f6aa* or winlog.event_data.Properties:*1131f6ad* or winlog.event_data.Properties:*9923a32a*) and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:(*$ or MSOL_* or manageengine or "ANONYMOUS LOGON")

name: AD — Domain Reconnaissance via LOLBins / BloodHound
description:
Attacker objective
Enumerate the domain — privileged groups, trusts, Domain Controllers and users — to plan privilege escalation and lateral movement.

Attack logic
After a foothold, attackers map Active Directory using built-in tools (nltest, net group, dsquery, wmic) or collectors (SharpHound/BloodHound). This enumeration precedes targeting of privileged accounts and trusts.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the recon tools and arguments; matching domain-enumeration and collector patterns isolates reconnaissance, independent of case.

False positives
An administrator legitimately querying group membership, trusts or DCs.

Tuning
Allowlist known administrative hosts/accounts; a burst of distinct recon commands from one host is higher-confidence.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Review the recon commands and the host/user; a cluster of enumeration from one host suggests hands-on reconnaissance.
2. Correlate with a preceding foothold (phishing/exploit) and watch the same host for follow-on privilege escalation or lateral movement.
false_positives: An administrator legitimately querying group membership, trusts or DCs.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*nltest*" AND (cl LIKE "*dclist*" OR cl LIKE "*domain_trusts*" OR cl LIKE "*dsgetdc*" OR cl LIKE "*trusted_domains*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*group*" AND (cl LIKE "*domain admins*" OR cl LIKE "*enterprise admins*" OR cl LIKE "*domain controllers*") AND cl LIKE "*/domain*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*whoami*" AND cl LIKE "*/all*")
   OR cl LIKE "*sharphound*" OR cl LIKE "*bloodhound*" OR cl LIKE "*invoke-bloodhound*" OR cl LIKE "*collectionmethod*"
   OR (cl LIKE "*adfind*" AND (cl LIKE "*objectcategory*" OR cl LIKE "*trustdmp*" OR cl LIKE "*-gcb*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*dsquery*" AND (cl LIKE "*-filter*" OR cl LIKE "* group*" OR cl LIKE "* user*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*wmic*" AND cl LIKE "*/node:*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: AD — Domain Trust Added/Removed or Domain Policy Modified
description: Domain-level trust or policy changes: 4706/4707 (trust created/removed), 4713 (Kerberos policy), 4716 (trust info modified), 4739 (domain policy changed — 65 events/90d measured, sole occurring code). These were buried inside QA - Windows Changes with no dedicated coverage. Low volume, high value: trust manipulation is a forest-compromise technique.
author: JCB Detection Engineering

name: AD — Group Policy Object Modified by an Unexpected Principal
description:
Attacker objective
Modify a Group Policy Object to push attacker configuration — a startup/logon script, a new local admin, a scheduled task, or a security-setting change — across many machines at once.

Attack logic
GPOs are edited by a small set of authorized administrators. A directory change to a groupPolicyContainer object by any other principal is anomalous and can deploy malicious configuration domain-wide.

Why this detection works
Directory-service change auditing (5136) records modifications to Group Policy objects with the acting principal; a new-terms model auto-baselines the known GPO editors and fires on any new one.

False positives
Onboarding of a new legitimate GPO administrator.

Tuning
Allowlist verified GPO administrators; correlate GPO edits with change control.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 5136 (ObjectClass=groupPolicyContainer, SubjectUserName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName is the (unexpected) principal editing a GPO; identify which GPO and what changed.
2. Verify against change control; a malicious GPO edit can deploy code or privileged accounts widely — revert and investigate urgently.
false_positives: Onboarding of a new legitimate GPO administrator.
query: event.code:"5136" and winlog.event_data.ObjectClass:"groupPolicyContainer"

name: AD — Kerberoasting: RC4 Service Ticket Requested
description:
Attacker objective
Request RC4 (0x17) Kerberos service tickets for SPN-bearing accounts to crack their passwords offline (Kerberoasting).

Attack logic
In an AES-enforced domain, RC4 service tickets are rare and belong to a few legacy accounts. An RC4 service-ticket request for any other account is an encryption downgrade characteristic of Kerberoasting tooling.

Why this detection works
Event 4769 records the ticket encryption type and the target service, so allowlisting known legacy RC4 accounts turns any other 0x17 service ticket into a high-signal event.

False positives
Additional legacy RC4-only service accounts.

Tuning
Add verified legacy accounts to the exclusion; investigate any RC4 request for a modern account.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4769 (TicketEncryptionType, ServiceName, TargetUserName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. TargetUserName = the requesting account; ServiceName = the SPN targeted.
2. An RC4 downgrade for a non-legacy service is Kerberoasting; reset the SPN account password (long/complex) and hunt for offline cracking follow-on.
false_positives: Additional legacy RC4-only service accounts.
query: event.code:"4769" and winlog.event_data.TicketEncryptionType:"0x17" and not winlog.event_data.ServiceName:"rpap" and not winlog.event_data.ServiceName:"krbtgt"

name: AD — Kerberos Brute Force Against a Single Account (4771 bad-password burst)
description: ≥20 Kerberos pre-auth failures with status 0x18 (bad password) against one account within 30 minutes. Complements the spray rule (which needs many accounts) by catching a targeted attack on one account. Expect near-zero noise once aml_srv/achuser/callcenter credential storms are fixed.
author: JCB Detection Engineering
query: event.code:"4771" and winlog.event_data.Status:"0x18" and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:*$

name: AD — Kerberos Replay Attack Detected
description: Windows event 4649 is logged when the Kerberos subsystem detects a replayed authenticator — the same request submitted twice. It is a direct indicator of ticket replay, pass-the-ticket and relay tooling, and it is one of the few Windows events that is almost never produced by normal operation. Validated baseline at JCB: 5 events across 7 days on a single host. No existing rule covers this event code.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Establish the account and host in the event, then review all Kerberos activity (4768/4769/4771) for that account around the same time.
2. A cluster of 4649 events, or 4649 on a domain controller or Tier-0 server, should be treated as active credential-material abuse.
3. Correlate with `Windows — Pass-the-Hash / Overpass-the-Hash Logon Pattern`, `AD — Kerberoasting: RC4 Service Ticket Requested` and `AD — DCSync: Directory Replication by an Unexpected Principal`.
4. Isolated single events can result from network retransmission — investigate but weigh volume and destination.
false_positives: Network-level packet duplication or an aggressive load balancer replaying authentication traffic.
Misbehaving application that caches and resubmits a Kerberos authenticator.
query: event.code:"4649"

name: AD — KRBTGT Account Password Reset (Golden Ticket Prep / Remediation)
description:
Attacker objective
A KRBTGT password reset is either Golden-Ticket remediation or attacker manipulation of the domain's Kerberos trust — a Tier-0 event that must be verified.

Attack logic
The KRBTGT account is not reset in normal operation. Any reset is a Tier-0 change to the domain's Kerberos master key.

Why this detection works
Password-reset events (4724/4723) targeting the krbtgt account are a zero-baseline tripwire.

False positives
A deliberate, scheduled KRBTGT rotation.

Tuning
Correlate with planned rotation activity and change control.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4724/4723 (TargetUserName=krbtgt, SubjectUserName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Confirm whether this is a planned rotation.
2. If not, investigate as potential Golden-Ticket activity and treat the domain as compromised until cleared.
false_positives: A deliberate, scheduled KRBTGT rotation.
query: event.code:("4724" or "4723" or "4738") and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:"krbtgt"

name: AD — KRBTGT Account Password Reset or Change
description: Detects a password reset (event 4724) or change (4723) on the KRBTGT account. The KRBTGT key signs all Kerberos tickets; resetting it is either a planned double-rotation or Golden Ticket remediation/attack activity.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` performed the reset on `krbtgt`.
2. Confirm this was an authorised, scheduled KRBTGT rotation (and that it was performed twice per Microsoft guidance).
3. If unplanned: a KRBTGT reset can indicate Golden Ticket remediation OR an attacker resetting to control ticket signing — investigate for prior DCSync / Domain Admin compromise.
## Response
If unauthorised: treat the domain as compromised; rotate KRBTGT twice, reset Tier-0 credentials, hunt for Golden Tickets.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:("4723" or "4724") and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:"krbtgt"

name: AD — Mass Group Enumeration via LOLBin (BloodHound/SharpHound)
description: Detects a scripting/LOLBin process (PowerShell, wmic, cmd, net, rundll32, cscript/wscript, mshta) enumerating 15+ security-enabled groups (4799) from a single host/account within an hour. This is the signature of BloodHound/SharpHound and manual AD reconnaissance. Enterprise software (Cluster, Veeam, Kaspersky, ManageEngine) and the known admin jump-host baseline are excluded, so the residual signal is anomalous group enumeration.
note:
## Investigation
1. `CallerProcessName` = the enumerating LOLBin; `SubjectUserName`/`host.name` = the actor.
2. A workstation/server (not an admin jump host) running PowerShell/net enumerating many groups rapidly = likely SharpHound. Pull the full process tree.
## Response
Isolate the host, identify the collector binary/script, and hunt for follow-on lateral movement / Kerberoasting.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"4799" and winlog.event_data.CallerProcessName:(*powershell* or *\\wmic.exe or *\\cmd.exe or *rundll32* or *cscript* or *wscript* or *mshta* or *\\net.exe or *\\net1.exe) and not (host.name:"nim-jump-apv22" and winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"jamal.admin")

name: AD — Member Added to Privileged Operators Group
description: Fires when an account is added to a built-in privileged operators group — Account (S-1-5-32-548), Server (549), Print (550), Backup (551), or Cryptographic (569) Operators — via events 4728/4732/4756. These groups are Tier-0-adjacent: Backup Operators can read NTDS.dit (DCSync-equivalent) and Server/Account Operators approach Domain Admin, so membership change is a common persistence/privilege-escalation step. Maps to ATT&CK Persistence T1098 (Account Manipulation).
note:
### Investigation
1. Identify the actor (SubjectUserName) and confirm they are authorized to modify these groups.
2. Identify the member added (MemberName) and which group (TargetSid) — Backup/Server/Account Operators are the highest concern.
3. Check for an approved change ticket covering this membership change.
4. Correlate the new member's subsequent activity (privileged logons, NTDS/backup access, DCSync) for abuse of the granted rights.
5. Escalate immediately if the change is unapproved or the member is an unexpected/newly created account.

### False positives / benign
Sanctioned admin or delegated onboarding legitimately adds Backup or Print Operators; legitimate but must be change-controlled. Distinguish by matching the actor, member, and group against an approved change record — not by allowlisting the actor. An add outside a change window, by an unexpected actor, or granting the most powerful groups (Server/Account/Backup Operators) is treated as malicious until proven otherwise.
author: raadabujaish

name: AD — Member Added to a Tier-0 Group (Domain/Enterprise/Schema Admins)
description: Detects a member being added to a Tier-0 Active Directory group — Domain Admins (-512), Enterprise Admins (-519), Schema Admins (-518), Domain Controllers (-516), Group Policy Creator Owners (-520) or built-in Administrators (S-1-5-32-544). Tier-0 group membership grants full domain control.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` (actor) added `MemberName`/`MemberSid` to the group `TargetUserName`.
2. Confirm the change is authorised (change ticket) and the actor is a legitimate Tier-0 admin.
3. Check whether the added member is a normal user, service account, or attacker-controlled account.
## Response
If unauthorised: remove the membership, disable the added account, and investigate the actor account for compromise.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:("4728" or "4756" or "4732") and winlog.event_data.TargetSid:(*-512 or *-519 or *-518 or *-516 or *-520 or "S-1-5-32-544")

name: AD — Member Added to a Privileged (Tier-0) Group
description:
Attacker objective
Gain domain dominance or persistence by adding an account to a highly-privileged group (Domain/Enterprise/Schema Admins, built-in Operators, or privileged Exchange groups).

Attack logic
Membership changes to Tier-0 groups are rare and among the most consequential directory changes. An addition to these groups grants far-reaching control and warrants verification.

Why this detection works
Group-membership events (4728/4756/4732) record the group, the added member and the acting subject.

False positives
Authorised administration.

Tuning
Correlate with change tickets; the local Administrators group can be noisier and can be split out if needed.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4728/4756/4732 (TargetUserName/group, MemberName, SubjectUserName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName added a member to a Tier-0 group; MemberName = who was added.
2. Verify authorisation; if unauthorised, remove the member and investigate the subject and the added account's subsequent activity.
false_positives: Authorised administration.
query: event.code:("4728" or "4756" or "4732") and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:("Domain Admins" or "Enterprise Admins" or "Schema Admins" or "Group Policy Creator Owners" or "DnsAdmins" or "Cert Publishers" or "Exchange Organization Administrators" or "Exchange Trusted Subsystem" or "Account Operators" or "Backup Operators" or "Server Operators" or "Administrators")

name: AD — Multi-SPN Roast then Service-Account Logon
description: A single source IP requested Kerberos service tickets (4769) for 2 or more distinct user service-principal-names and then authenticated (4624 type 3/10) as 3 or more distinct service accounts — the roast-and-use pattern where an attacker Kerberoasts SPNs, cracks the tickets offline, and replays the recovered service-account credentials. The rule correlates 4769 TGS requests and 4624 logons by source.ip. Maps to ATT&CK Credential Access T1558.003 (Kerberoasting) into Lateral Movement.
note:
### Investigation
1. List the roasted SPNs (ServiceName) and the accounts subsequently used — do the requested SPNs match the accounts logged on as?
2. Check RC4 (etype 0x17) on the 4769s, which strengthens the Kerberoast hypothesis.
3. Determine whether source.ip is a legitimate multi-service application/broker host (Citrix, integration server) that naturally uses several service accounts.
4. Pivot to the destination hosts of the 4624 logons for privileged access or fan-out.
5. Escalate if the SPNs are high-value/Tier-0 accounts and the source is not a sanctioned application host.

### False positives / benign
Multi-service application and broker hosts (Citrix, integration/middleware servers) legitimately request tickets for and authenticate as several service accounts, matching the roast-and-use shape. Distinguish by whether the requested SPNs correspond to the host's known application role, whether ticket encryption is normal (AES vs RC4-downgrade), and by resolving the source against known_infrastructure — not by allowlisting the IP, which would blind the analytic to an attacker on that segment.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Multi-service application/broker hosts (e.g. Citrix, integration servers) that legitimately request and use several service accounts — validate and suppress by source.ip.
query:
FROM logs-system.security-*
| WHERE (event.code=="4769" AND source.ip IS NOT NULL AND source.ip != "::1") OR (event.code=="4624" AND winlog.event_data.LogonType IN ("3","10"))
| EVAL sname=TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.ServiceName), tl = TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName),
       is_usr_spn = (event.code=="4769" AND NOT sname LIKE "*$*" AND NOT sname LIKE "*/*" AND sname != "krbtgt"),
       is_svc_logon = (event.code=="4624" AND (tl LIKE "*.admin" OR tl LIKE "*sys_user" OR tl LIKE "*.servacc" OR tl LIKE "*.prod" OR tl LIKE "*.srv" OR tl LIKE "icbs*" OR tl LIKE "sigcap*" OR tl LIKE "forti.*" OR tl LIKE "custody*" OR tl LIKE "citrix*" OR tl LIKE "docsafe" OR tl LIKE "wss.user" OR tl LIKE "sp.admin" OR tl LIKE "solarwinds*" OR tl LIKE "veeam*" OR tl LIKE "sccm*" OR tl LIKE "named*" OR tl LIKE "ps" OR tl LIKE "pam" OR tl LIKE "igrafxsso*" OR tl LIKE "office365" OR tl LIKE "internal.services" OR tl LIKE "innscanservice" OR tl LIKE "teammatese" OR tl LIKE "filenet*" OR tl LIKE "los.test" OR tl LIKE "aml.eod" OR tl LIKE "cms" OR tl LIKE "vynamic*" OR tl LIKE "svc*" OR tl LIKE "*service*" OR tl LIKE "*_svc" OR tl LIKE "backup*" OR tl LIKE "oracle*" OR tl LIKE "sql*"))
| STATS roasted_spns=COUNT_DISTINCT(CASE(is_usr_spn, winlog.event_data.ServiceName, null)),
        svc_logon_ids=COUNT_DISTINCT(CASE(is_svc_logon, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName, null)),
        roasted=VALUES(CASE(is_usr_spn, winlog.event_data.ServiceName, null)),
        used=VALUES(CASE(is_svc_logon, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName, null)),
        first_seen=MIN(@timestamp), last_seen=MAX(@timestamp) BY source.ip
| WHERE roasted_spns >= 2 AND svc_logon_ids >= 3
| SORT roasted_spns DESC

name: AD — New Computer (Machine) Account Created
description: Detects creation of a new Active Directory computer account (event 4741). Attacker-created machine accounts underpin resource-based constrained delegation abuse and the sAMAccountName-spoofing / noPac (CVE-2021-42278) attack chain.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` created the computer `TargetUserName`.
2. Machine accounts are normally created by Domain Admins or during domain join — a standard user creating one (default MachineAccountQuota=10) is suspicious.
3. Check for subsequent RBCD/SPN changes or noPac renaming on this computer object.
## Response
If unauthorised: delete the computer object and investigate the creating account.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"4741"

name: AD — New Computer (Machine) Account Created
description:
Attacker objective
Create a machine account for resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) abuse, DCShadow, or as a stealthy foothold.

Attack logic
Computer-account creation is low-volume and is abused in several modern AD attacks. Creation by a non-standard principal is higher-risk.

Why this detection works
Event 4741 records machine-account creation with the acting subject and the new account.

False positives
Legitimate device onboarding/imaging.

Tuning
Allowlist provisioning accounts; prioritise creation by non-standard principals.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4741 (SubjectUserName, TargetUserName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName created TargetUserName (the machine account).
2. Confirm it maps to a real device onboarding, not RBCD/DCShadow preparation; watch for a subsequent msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity write on a target host.
false_positives: Legitimate device onboarding/imaging.
query: event.code:"4741"

name: AD — New Directory Replication Principal
description: Detects a directory-replication principal — an identity performing DS-Replication-Get-Changes / Get-Changes-All / Get-Changes-In-Filtered-Set on a domain controller (Windows 4662, control-access GUIDs 1131f6aa / 1131f6ad / 89e95b76) — whose SID has NOT been seen replicating in the last 90 days. Granting a controlled account directory-replication rights is the classic DCSync setup step (T1003.006). At NBI the entire 90-day replicator population is four stable identities (Azure AD Connect, two DC machine accounts, and sanctioned directory-read accounts); a fifth, new replicator is inherently high-signal. Keyed on the stable SID (not the account name) so an attacker cannot evade by naming the account into an allowlist, and rate-agnostic (New Terms) so a single replication still fires. 4662 carries no network source IP — origin is the DC that logged it (host.name) plus the actor SID; correlate 4624/4768 for the source host.
note:
### Triage — new directory-replication principal
1. **WHO** `winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName` / `SubjectUserSid` — a newly-sanctioned tool (backup/sync/monitoring) or an unexpected account? Confirm with the AD team whether replication rights were just granted, and by whom.
2. **WHAT** `winlog.event_data.Properties` — which right? `*1131f6ad*` (Get-Changes-**ALL**) = can extract secrets → treat as **critical** (see the Get-Changes-All companion rule). `*1131f6aa*`/`*89e95b76*` only = directory-metadata read.
3. **FROM WHERE** 4662 has no source IP — pivot the actor SID into 4624/4768 around this time to find the source host/IP. A replication principal authenticating from a workstation is suspicious.
4. **Escalate** if rights were not deliberately granted, the account is a normal user/computer, or Get-Changes-ALL is present. De-escalate only after the AD team confirms a sanctioned replicator — then add its **SID** (never its name) to the approved-replicator `known_infrastructure` list.

standard.logic_explanation: New Terms on SubjectUserSid over 4662 DCSync control-access GUIDs; 90d history; fires on a never-before-seen replicator SID.

query: event.code:"4662" and winlog.event_data.Properties:(*1131f6aa* or *1131f6ad* or *89e95b76*)

name: AD — NTLM Authentication Fan-Out
description: A single source IP used NTLM to authenticate (network logon type 3) to 8 or more distinct hosts within 6 hours — the fan-out signature of Pass-the-Hash or credential replay spreading across the estate. The rule aggregates 4624 NTLM logons per source.ip and counts distinct destination hosts and identities. Attackers replay a stolen NTLM hash from one foothold to reach many machines quickly. Maps to ATT&CK Lateral Movement T1550.002 (Pass the Hash) with T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares).
note:
### Investigation
1. Review dest_hosts and accounts — one identity spraying many hosts, or many identities from one source (both suspicious)?
2. Determine whether source.ip is a sanctioned mgmt/patch/EDR/PAM node (known_infrastructure) that legitimately reaches many endpoints.
3. Pivot on the accounts used and check whether NTLM (not Kerberos) is expected for those hosts — NTLM where Kerberos is normal strengthens PtH.
4. Correlate follow-on 5140/5145 admin-share access and any 4672 on the destinations.
5. Escalate if the source is not an inventoried management host and the accounts are privileged.

### False positives / benign
Management, patch (SCCM), EDR, and PAM push hosts legitimately fan out NTLM to many endpoints — the baseline names mgmt 10.11.18.21/.49 and PAM 10.11.102.15 reaching 13-18 hosts. Distinguish by resolving source.ip against a known_infrastructure management group and by identity profile: sanctioned tooling uses a stable service account to a predictable host set, whereas PtH shows a user/admin credential reaching an unusual or growing set. Baseline the known pushers rather than raising the threshold, which would let a slow attacker under it.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Management/patch/EDR servers and PAM that legitimately push to many endpoints via NTLM (validate then suppress by source.ip).
query:
FROM logs-system.security-*
| WHERE event.code == "4624" AND winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" AND winlog.event_data.AuthenticationPackageName == "NTLM" AND source.ip IS NOT NULL AND source.ip != "::1"
| STATS ntlm_logons=COUNT(*), dest_hosts=COUNT_DISTINCT(host.name), identities=COUNT_DISTINCT(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), accounts=VALUES(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), first_seen=MIN(@timestamp), last_seen=MAX(@timestamp) BY source.ip
| WHERE dest_hosts >= 8
| SORT dest_hosts DESC

name: AD — Object Security Descriptor Modified (DACL Backdoor)
description:
Attacker objective
Grant stealthy rights (DCSync/GenericAll/WriteDACL) on an AD object for persistence or escalation by modifying its security descriptor.

Attack logic
Security-descriptor changes on directory objects are normally system-driven (for example AdminSDHolder propagation under the SYSTEM context). Human-driven descriptor changes — especially on Tier-0 objects — can plant an ACL backdoor such as replication (DCSync) rights.

Why this detection works
Event 5136 records nTSecurityDescriptor modifications with the acting subject, so excluding SYSTEM isolates human-driven ACL changes.

False positives
Authorised delegation changes.

Tuning
Correlate with change control; pay special attention to grants of replication (DCSync), GenericAll or WriteDACL rights.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 5136 (AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName changed the ACL of ObjectDN.
2. Inspect the added ACE (DCSync / GenericAll / WriteDACL) and remove it if malicious; investigate the subject.
false_positives: Authorised delegation changes.
query: event.code:"5136" and winlog.event_data.AttributeLDAPDisplayName:"nTSecurityDescriptor" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"SYSTEM"

name: AD — Object Security Descriptor Modified (DACL backdoor)
description: Detects modification of the nTSecurityDescriptor (DACL) on an Active Directory object. Attackers grant themselves rights such as DCSync (Replicating Directory Changes), GenericAll, or WriteDACL to establish stealthy, ACL-based persistence and escalation. Note: AdminSDHolder propagation legitimately rewrites descriptors on protected objects — correlate the subject and target.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` = who changed the ACL; `ObjectDN` = the object whose rights changed.
2. Rule out AdminSDHolder/SYSTEM propagation. Human-driven descriptor changes on Tier-0 objects (domain root, AdminSDHolder, privileged groups) are the concern.
## Response
Inspect the granted ACE; if a backdoor right was added, remove it and investigate the subject.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"5136" and winlog.event_data.AttributeLDAPDisplayName:"nTSecurityDescriptor" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"SYSTEM"

name: AD — Repeated Authentication Against Disabled or Locked Accounts
description: ≥10 authentication attempts in 30 minutes from one source against DISABLED/LOCKED/EXPIRED accounts (4771 0x12; 4625 substatus 0xC0000072/0xC0000234/0xC0000193). Valid credentials are dead — repeated use indicates orphaned services or an attacker replaying stolen credentials.
author: JCB Detection Engineering
query: (event.code:"4771" and winlog.event_data.Status:"0x12") or (event.code:"4625" and winlog.event_data.SubStatus:("0xc0000072" or "0xc0000234" or "0xc0000193"))

name: AD — Service Ticket for Sensitive Service Account
description: Intended to fire when a Kerberos service ticket (4769) is requested for a service account on a sensitive/Tier-0 watchlist — the request step of Kerberoasting, where an attacker obtains a TGS to crack the service account's password offline. It should key on the requested ServiceName matching a known_infrastructure high-value-SPN group, ideally combined with RC4 ticket encryption. Maps to ATT&CK Credential Access T1558.003 (Kerberoasting). The deployed query is just event.code 4769 and matches every ticket request (~2.06M/24h) — it must be re-scoped before use.
note:
### Investigation
1. Confirm the requested ServiceName is a sensitive/Tier-0 service account (resolve against the known_infrastructure watchlist).
2. Check TicketEncryptionType — RC4 (0x17) on a high-value SPN is a strong Kerberoast indicator versus normal AES traffic.
3. Identify the requesting account (TargetUserName) and source.ip; is this host/user a normal consumer of that service?
4. Correlate a burst of 4769s for many SPNs from the same source (bulk roasting) and any follow-on logon as the service account.
5. Escalate if a Tier-0 SPN is requested with RC4 from an unexpected source.

### False positives / benign
As currently written there is no discriminator, so every normal Kerberos logon matches — a logic defect, not a benign-traffic problem. Once scoped to the sensitive-SPN watchlist, legitimate consumers of those services still request tickets normally; distinguish real roasting by RC4 encryption downgrade, bulk multi-SPN requests from one source, and requests from hosts that are not normal clients of the service — not by allowlisting.

### Notes
LOGIC DEFECT (pending Batch-2 rewrite): deployed query matches all 4769 (~2M/24h); scope to the sensitive-SPN watchlist + RC4 before relying on it.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Application servers that legitimately host these service accounts (validate the source.ip, then suppress the account+source pair).
query: event.code:"4769"

name: AD — Service/Privileged Account Logon from Novel Source
description: A privileged or service account authenticated over the network (logon type 3) or via RDP (type 10) from a source IP it has never used in the last 30 days. Attackers who steal service-account credentials or hashes replay them from their own foothold, so a novel source for a high-value identity is an early lateral-movement signal. The rule uses a New Terms detection on the (TargetUserName, source.ip) pair, scoped to accounts matching NBI's service/privileged naming patterns. Maps to ATT&CK Lateral Movement T1078.002 (Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts).
note:
### Investigation
1. Confirm the account is genuinely privileged/service and identify its normal source hosts from prior 4624 history.
2. Pivot on source.ip — a known admin jump host, PAM node, or patch server, or an unrecognized/user-subnet address?
3. Correlate host.name for follow-on 5140/5145 share access or 4672 special privileges, and any type-3 fan-out from the same source.
4. Check for preceding 4776/NTLM or 4769 activity for this account suggesting credential theft or replay.
5. Escalate if the source is unrecognized AND the account touches a sensitive asset (resolve host via known_infrastructure, not a name guess).

### False positives / benign
A service account brought online on a new application, patch, or migration host legitimately produces a novel (account, source.ip) pair. Distinguish by whether the new source is an inventoried server in a change window and whether the account keeps authenticating from it (sustained, single-purpose) versus a one-off logon from a workstation/user subnet followed by fan-out. The 30-day New Terms window suppresses recurring sources but new infrastructure still fires, so correlate to change tickets rather than allowlisting the IP.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"4624" and (winlog.event_data.LogonType:"3" or winlog.event_data.LogonType:"10") and source.ip:* and not source.ip:"::1" and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:(*Srv or *.admin or *sys_user or ICBS* or SIGCAP* or Sigcap* or *.servacc or *.prod or Docsafe or CITRIX* or Forti* or custody* or Solarwinds* or Veeam* or SCCM* or SP.admin)

name: AD — Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink modified)
description: Detects modification of the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute on an Active Directory object. Writing a Key Credential enables certificate/PKINIT-based authentication as the target (Shadow Credentials / Whisker / ESC) — a stealthy takeover and persistence primitive. This attribute changes rarely in normal operation, so any modification warrants review.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` = who wrote the key credential; `ObjectDN` = the victim account (user or computer).
2. Legitimate writers are limited (Windows Hello for Business provisioning). Confirm the subject is authorised.
## Response
If unauthorised, remove the added KeyCredential, reset the affected account, and investigate the subject for compromise.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:("5136" or "5137") and winlog.event_data.AttributeLDAPDisplayName:"msDS-KeyCredentialLink"

name: AD — Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink Modified)
description:
Attacker objective
Write a Key Credential (msDS-KeyCredentialLink) to an account to authenticate as it via PKINIT (Shadow Credentials / Whisker) — stealthy takeover and persistence.

Attack logic
This attribute is written only during legitimate key-based credential provisioning (for example Windows Hello for Business). A modification outside that process enables certificate-based impersonation of the target account.

Why this detection works
Directory-service change auditing (5136/5137) records modifications to msDS-KeyCredentialLink with the acting subject and the target object.

False positives
Legitimate Windows Hello for Business enrollment.

Tuning
Allowlist the WHfB provisioning service/account.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 5136/5137 (AttributeLDAPDisplayName=msDS-KeyCredentialLink, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName wrote the key credential; ObjectDN = the victim account.
2. Remove the KeyCredential, reset the target account, and investigate the subject and any PKINIT logons that followed.
false_positives: Legitimate Windows Hello for Business enrollment.
query: event.code:("5136" or "5137") and winlog.event_data.AttributeLDAPDisplayName:"msDS-KeyCredentialLink"

name: AD — SPN Added by Non-Computer Principal (Kerberoast Setup)
description:
Attacker objective
Set a Service Principal Name on an account (especially a user account) to make it Kerberoastable.

Attack logic
Computer accounts self-register SPNs and are excluded. A human or service principal adding an SPN — particularly to a user account — is a Kerberoast-setup pattern that precedes an RC4/service-ticket request.

Why this detection works
Event 5136 records servicePrincipalName additions with the acting subject, so excluding computer principals isolates the setup behaviour.

False positives
Administrative service-account provisioning.

Tuning
Allowlist provisioning admins; an SPN added to a user account is highest-risk.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 5136 (AttributeLDAPDisplayName=servicePrincipalName, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName added the SPN; ObjectDN = the account.
2. If the target is a user account, rotate its password and watch for a subsequent RC4 service-ticket request.
false_positives: Administrative service-account provisioning.
query: event.code:"5136" and winlog.event_data.AttributeLDAPDisplayName:"servicePrincipalName" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$ and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"SYSTEM"

name: AD — SPN Added by Non-Computer Principal (Kerberoast setup)
description: Detects a servicePrincipalName being set on an account by a non-computer (human/service) principal. Computer accounts self-register SPNs routinely (excluded here); a human adding an SPN — especially to a user account — is a classic Kerberoasting setup, making the account's password hash requestable and crackable offline.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` = who added the SPN; `ObjectDN` = the account that received it.
2. An SPN added to a *user* account is high-risk. Confirm against change control.
## Response
If unauthorised, remove the SPN and rotate the target account's password (long/complex to resist offline cracking).
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"5136" and winlog.event_data.AttributeLDAPDisplayName:"servicePrincipalName" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$ and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"SYSTEM" and not winlog.event_data.ObjectDN:*CN=Computers* and not winlog.event_data.ObjectDN:*Domain Controllers*

name: AD — Directory Sync Account Sign-In From New Source
description: Companion to the DCSync detections. The Azure AD Connect sync account (MSOL_cb8d5eb8df87) is the one identity legitimately permitted to replicate directory secrets (Get-Changes-ALL). Over 90 days it authenticates from exactly one host — the AAD Connect server 10.11.18.16 (source.ip 100% populated). This rule (New Terms on source.ip, scoped to that account, 4624/4768) fires when the sync account authenticates from any OTHER source — i.e. its credentials/token were stolen and reused elsewhere. It closes the residual left by the Get-Changes-ALL rule, which allowlists the sync account: if the sync account itself is abused from a different host, this fires. Residual blind spot: abuse of the sync account FROM 10.11.18.16 itself (e.g. mimikatz on that server) produces no source novelty and requires host-level EDR on 10.11.18.16, which is not currently proven in NBI telemetry (recorded as a NO_TELEMETRY gap).
note:
### Triage — Azure AD Connect sync account from a new source
1. **WHO / to WHAT** `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` = `MSOL_cb8d5eb8df87` (the directory-secret-capable sync account).
2. **FROM WHERE (discriminator)** `source.ip` — any value other than the canonical AAD Connect server `10.11.18.16`. This should never happen in normal operation.
3. **WHAT** 4624/4768 authentication (`event.code`, `winlog.logon.type`).
4. **Escalate:** treat as potential theft of the AAD Connect account. Correlate with the Get-Changes-ALL rule — if this account also replicated secrets from the new host, it is an active DCSync. First rule out a legitimate AAD Connect server migration/failover that changed the IP.

standard.logic_explanation: New Terms on source.ip for the AAD Connect account's 4624/4768; fires on a source IP other than 10.11.18.16.
standard.residual_gap: abuse from 10.11.18.16 itself needs host EDR (NO_TELEMETRY)

query: event.code:("4624" or "4768") and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:"MSOL_cb8d5eb8df87" and source.ip:*

name: AD — Unauthorized Directory Secret Replication
description: Detects extraction of directory SECRETS via replication — DS-Replication-Get-Changes-ALL (control-access GUID 1131f6ad, Windows 4662) — by any identity other than the sanctioned Azure AD Connect sync account (SID …-18109) and other than a DC's own SYSTEM context (S-1-5-18). Get-Changes-ALL is the specific right that permits reading password hashes/secrets; it is what mimikatz/impacket 'dcsync' requires. At NBI, over 30 days, ONLY Azure AD Connect exercises this right (43,278 events) — no other identity does. Any non-sync identity performing Get-Changes-ALL is therefore unsanctioned secret extraction (DCSync). This covers the compromised-approved-account case: an account approved only for Get-Changes (directory read) that escalates to Get-Changes-ALL to steal secrets fires here even though its SID is already known. Excludes the AAD Connect SID (legitimate password-hash sync) and S-1-5-18 (a DC replicating as SYSTEM — a SYSTEM-level DC compromise is a separate, higher-order incident under Tier-0 controls, and this exclusion removes zero current events).
note:
### Triage — unsanctioned directory secret replication (DCSync)
1. **WHO** `SubjectUserName`/`SubjectUserSid` — this identity pulled directory **secrets** (Get-Changes-ALL). The only sanctioned secret-puller at NBI is Azure AD Connect (`MSOL_cb8d5eb8df87`). Anything else is credential theft by default.
2. **WHAT / to WHAT** Get-Changes-ALL (Properties contains `1131f6ad`) against DC `host.name`.
3. **FROM WHERE** 4662 logs no source IP — immediately pivot the actor SID into 4624/4768 for the source host; confirm whether it is a workstation/server that should never replicate.
4. **Escalate immediately (critical):** assume domain-credential compromise. Rotate krbtgt twice, reset exposed privileged credentials, and hunt the source host. Not a tuning candidate — if it is a newly-sanctioned sync tool, confirm and add its SID to the approved secret-capable list explicitly.

standard.logic_explanation: Query on 4662 Get-Changes-ALL (1131f6ad) excluding the AAD Connect SID and S-1-5-18; the secret-extraction right by a non-sync identity.
standard.severity_rationale: Impact 3 (domain secret extraction) x Fidelity 3 (only Azure AD Connect legitimately uses Get-Changes-ALL) x Actionability 3 = critical.
standard.covers_evasion: compromised Get-Changes-only approved account escalating to Get-Changes-ALL

query: event.code:"4662" and winlog.event_data.Properties:*1131f6ad* and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserSid:"S-1-5-21-3845771475-482288069-3644183667-18109" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserSid:"S-1-5-18"

name: AD/Windows — Audit Policy Changed by Interactive Account
description:
Attacker objective
Disable audit subcategories to blind the SOC.

Attack logic
Audit-policy changes are normally applied by the machine/SYSTEM context via Group Policy. A change made under an interactive (human) account is anomalous.

Why this detection works
Event 4719 records audit-policy changes with the acting subject, so excluding machine/SYSTEM isolates human-driven changes.

False positives
An authorised interactive administrative change.

Tuning
Correlate with change control; investigate any interactive audit-policy change.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4719 (SubjectUserName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. An interactive account changed audit policy.
2. Verify authorisation; attackers disable auditing to evade detection — check what subcategory was disabled and on which host.
false_positives: An authorised interactive administrative change.
query: event.code:"4719" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$ and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("SYSTEM" or "LOCAL SERVICE" or "NETWORK SERVICE")

name: AD/Windows — Security Event Log Cleared
description:
Attacker objective
Erase forensic evidence by clearing the Windows Security event log.

Attack logic
Clearing the Security log is not part of normal operations. Any occurrence is a classic anti-forensics step, frequently seen after hands-on-keyboard activity.

Why this detection works
Event 1102 is emitted whenever the Security log is cleared, and records the acting subject.

False positives
Authorised administrative maintenance (rare).

Tuning
Correlate with maintenance windows and change control.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 1102 (SubjectUserName, computer).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SubjectUserName cleared the log on the named host.
2. Verify authorisation; log clearing is a strong compromise indicator — pivot to other telemetry for the same host/time window.
false_positives: Authorised administrative maintenance (rare).
query: event.code:"1102"

name: Potential Kerberoasting — Account Requesting Service Tickets for Many Distinct Service Accounts (4769)
description: Detects a single (non-machine) account requesting Kerberos service tickets (Event ID 4769) for an abnormally high number of DISTINCT non-machine service accounts within one hour — the behavioral signature of bulk Kerberoasting (Rubeus/Impacket GetUserSPNs/SharpHound). Defender-INDEPENDENT native detection: NBI is AES-only (4769 encryption is 100% 0x12 AES256, zero 0x17 RC4), so the classic RC4-downgrade Kerberoasting signature is structurally blind here; this rule instead keys on distinct-SPN cardinality, which holds regardless of encryption. Baseline (measured live): a non-machine account requesting tickets for distinct non-machine service accounts is <=3/day for every legitimate account; threshold set to >=10 distinct/hour for wide margin. Portable About: any tenant forwarding Windows Security 4769 to logs-system.security-*; excludes machine (`*$`) requesters/services and `krbtgt` to isolate user-service-account roasting.
note:
## Triage
1. `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` = the requesting account (potential roaster).
2. Pull its 4769 events; list the distinct `winlog.event_data.ServiceName` values = the roasted service accounts.
3. Bulk requests for many user-service SPNs in seconds/minutes = Kerberoasting. Reset/rotate the exposed service-account passwords.
4. Note: IpAddress is not populated on NBI 4769 — pivot on the account and correlate with Defender/MDI Kerberoasting alerts (see the Defender Credential-Access rule).
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Vulnerability scanners / identity-hygiene tools that enumerate SPNs (validate the account and schedule).
Authorized penetration tests.
query: event.code:"4769" and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:*$* and not winlog.event_data.ServiceName:*$* and not winlog.event_data.ServiceName:*/* and not winlog.event_data.ServiceName:krbtgt*

name: Credential Access — RC4 (0x17) Kerberos Ticket in an AES-Only Domain (Downgrade / Roast / Forged Ticket)
description: A Kerberos TGT/TGS (4768/4769) used RC4-HMAC (0x17). NBIRQ.COM is AES-only (baseline RC4 = 0), so RC4 is anomalous: Kerberoast downgrade, overpass-the-hash, or a forged (Golden/Silver) ticket. Objective: 0-baseline encryption-downgrade tripwire.
note:
### Investigation
1. Which account/service and source? RC4 should not occur in this domain.
2. If ServiceName=krbtgt-like or ticket lifetime anomalous → suspect Golden/Silver ticket.
3. Confirm the client/host is not a legacy system reintroducing RC4.
### Tuning
If a legitimate legacy system is found, allowlist that specific host after remediation planning; do not broaden.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: A newly introduced legacy system negotiating RC4 (should be remediated, not permanently allowlisted).
query: event.code:"4769" and winlog.event_data.TicketEncryptionType:"0x17" and not winlog.event_data.ServiceName:"krbtgt"

name: Lateral Movement — Single Source Authenticating as Many Distinct Service/Privileged Accounts
description: One source successfully authenticates (network/RDP) as an unusually large number of distinct service/privileged accounts within 6h — credential-replay lateral movement using harvested service creds (the confirmed Kali pattern: 28 identities).
note:
### Investigation
1. `svc_accounts` list — do these belong together operationally?
2. Is source.ip an application broker (Citrix/PAM) or a workstation/Kali/jump?
### Tuning
Legit multi-account brokers (Citrix VDI 10.11.101.x, PAM 10.11.102.x) may use many accounts — VALIDATE and suppress those specific source.ips; do not lower sensitivity blindly.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Citrix/VDI and PAM brokers that legitimately front many service accounts — validate and suppress by source.ip.
query:
FROM logs-system.security-*
| WHERE event.code=="4624" AND winlog.event_data.LogonType IN ("3","10") AND source.ip IS NOT NULL AND source.ip != "::1"
| EVAL tl=TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.TargetUserName), is_svc=(tl LIKE "*.admin" OR tl LIKE "*sys_user" OR tl LIKE "*.servacc" OR tl LIKE "*.prod" OR tl LIKE "*.srv" OR tl LIKE "icbs*" OR tl LIKE "sigcap*" OR tl LIKE "forti.*" OR tl LIKE "custody*" OR tl LIKE "citrix*" OR tl LIKE "docsafe" OR tl LIKE "wss.user" OR tl LIKE "sp.admin" OR tl LIKE "solarwinds*" OR tl LIKE "veeam*" OR tl LIKE "sccm*" OR tl LIKE "named*" OR tl LIKE "ps" OR tl LIKE "pam" OR tl LIKE "igrafxsso*" OR tl LIKE "office365" OR tl LIKE "internal.services" OR tl LIKE "innscanservice" OR tl LIKE "teammatese" OR tl LIKE "filenet*" OR tl LIKE "los.test" OR tl LIKE "aml.eod" OR tl LIKE "cms" OR tl LIKE "vynamic*" OR tl LIKE "svc*" OR tl LIKE "*service*" OR tl LIKE "*_svc" OR tl LIKE "backup*" OR tl LIKE "oracle*" OR tl LIKE "sql*")
| STATS svc_identities=COUNT_DISTINCT(CASE(is_svc, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName, null)), dest_hosts=COUNT_DISTINCT(host.name),
        svc_accounts=VALUES(CASE(is_svc, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName, null)), first_seen=MIN(@timestamp), last_seen=MAX(@timestamp) BY source.ip
| WHERE svc_identities >= 10
| SORT svc_identities DESC

name: Windows — New Interactive RDP Logon to a Host
description: Alerts the first time a given user account logs on interactively over RDP (logon type 10) to a given host, measured against a rolling 14-day history. RDP is tightly restricted at JCB — only 358 type-10 logons across 75 hosts in 7 days — which makes a previously unseen user/host RDP pair a strong lateral-movement signal rather than background noise. No existing rule covers RDP logon type 10.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Confirm the user/host pair against the expected administrative model: does this person normally administer this server?
2. Recover `source.ip` from the event to establish where the session originated; an RDP session sourced from a workstation subnet into the server estate, or from a server into another server, is the classic RDP-chaining pattern.
3. Review what the account did after logon: process creation (4688), service installs, and share access on the destination.
4. Correlate with `Windows — Potential SharpRDP Behavior` and with FortiGate traffic for RDP crossing network zones.
false_positives: A new administrator or a role change legitimately introducing a new user/host pair.
Server migrations and commissioning activity.
Helpdesk staff covering an unfamiliar system for the first time.
query: event.code:"4624" and winlog.event_data.LogonType:"10"

name: Windows — Pass-the-Hash / Overpass-the-Hash Logon Pattern
description:
Attacker objective
Authenticate with a stolen NTLM hash or Kerberos key instead of a password (Pass-the-Hash / Overpass-the-Hash) to impersonate a user.

Attack logic
Tools such as Mimikatz sekurlsa::pth create a logon session with alternate credentials. This produces a distinctive new-credentials (type 9) logon via the seclogo logon process using the Negotiate package — a fingerprint that legitimate runas/network logons do not match.

Why this detection works
Logon auditing (4624) records the logon type, logon process and authentication package; the specific type-9 + seclogo + Negotiate combination isolates the pass-the-hash pattern.

False positives
Some legitimate 'run as different user with network credentials' scenarios; verify the account and process context.

Tuning
Baseline any legitimate tooling that produces this pattern and allowlist it; investigate unexpected occurrences.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4624 (LogonType, LogonProcessName, AuthenticationPackageName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the target account and the host; a seclogo type-9 Negotiate logon is the classic pass-the-hash fingerprint.
2. Correlate with the process that initiated it (Mimikatz-style tooling) and the source host.
3. If confirmed, rotate the impersonated account's credentials and treat the host as compromised.
false_positives: Some legitimate 'run as different user with network credentials' scenarios; verify the account and process context.
query: event.code:"4624" and winlog.event_data.LogonType:"9" and winlog.event_data.LogonProcessName:"seclogo" and winlog.event_data.AuthenticationPackageName:"Negotiate"

name: Cisco IOS — Login Brute Force Against Device
description: Fires when a single Cisco IOS device logs 30 or more 'Login failed' syslog messages within an hour — the management-interface brute-force signature, against a baseline of roughly 2-3 failures/day. Attackers guess VTY/console/enable credentials to gain device control and pivot or alter routing. Implemented as a Threshold rule grouped by device hostname. Maps to ATT&CK Credential Access T1110 (Brute Force).
note:
### Investigation
1. Confirm the failure burst is concentrated on one device (log.syslog.hostname) and exceeds its normal ~2-3/day baseline.
2. Identify the source (log.source.address or the address embedded in message) — a known NMS/backup poller or an unexpected host?
3. Check for a subsequent successful login from the same source after the failures (compromise).
4. Correlate other devices hit by the same source (estate-wide credential attack).
5. Escalate on success-after-failures or an unrecognized source targeting management planes.

### False positives / benign
Monitoring/NMS churn and a mis-scheduled backup or poller with stale credentials can produce sustained 'Login failed' bursts from a fixed, known source. Distinguish by whether log.source.address is an inventoried management system (known_infrastructure) and whether a success ever follows — legitimate pollers fail consistently without succeeding interactively, whereas an attack often ends in a success or rotates usernames. Fix the stale-credential source rather than allowlisting the device.

### Notes
BLOCKED_BY_TELEMETRY: Cisco IOS @timestamp is future-dated; the rule cannot fire until the ingestion clock is fixed.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"cisco_ios.log" and message:"Login failed"

name: Cisco IOS — Manual Network Device Configuration Change
description: Detects a manual running-configuration change on a Cisco network device (%SYS-5-CONFIG_I = configured from console/vty by an operator), excluding automated NETCONF/controller pushes. Config changes on the ATM/branch network are high-impact and are a common step in network-level attacks (ACL/route tampering, adding access).
note:
## Investigation
1. `log.syslog.hostname` is the device (ATM/branch site); `message` shows the source line (console/vty/user).
2. Confirm the change against network change control.
## Response
If unauthorised, review the device running-config diff and investigate the source.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"cisco_ios.log" and message:"SYS-5-CONFIG_I"

name: CORE — New Database Principal Accessing Core Banking
description:
Attacker objective
Access or manipulate the core-banking database with a new or compromised account — a principal that does not normally touch the core banking schema.

Attack logic
The core-banking database is accessed by a very small, fixed set of service and application principals. A principal not seen before performing any operation against the core banking audit trail is a strong anomaly — a new service account, a misconfiguration, or a compromised/rogue identity reaching the crown-jewel database.

Why this detection works
A new-terms model over the database principal auto-baselines the known core-banking accounts and fires only on a genuinely new one.

False positives
Onboarding of a new legitimate core-banking service/application account.

Tuning
Verify and allowlist new legitimate principals; correlate the new principal's source and the operations it performed against the core banking database.

Required telemetry
Core banking database audit (apps-*, type=CORE_AuditTrail): USERNAME, ACTION_NAME, SQL_TEXT.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. USERNAME = the new database principal; review ACTION_NAME and SQL_TEXT for what it did.
2. Confirm whether the principal was legitimately onboarded; a new actor on the core banking database is high-risk.
3. Correlate with the source host/application and with any privileged operations.
false_positives: Onboarding of a new legitimate core-banking service/application account.
query: type:"CORE_AuditTrail" and USERNAME:*

name: Correlation — Compromised Endpoint with Active Data Exfiltration
description:
Attacker objective
Operate a compromised endpoint and steal data from it — the same host shows both an active compromise (malware, behavioral block, network attack, or a Windows/AD attack technique) and a data-loss-prevention exfiltration event.

Attack logic
A malware or behavioral detection on a host is a compromise signal; a DLP incident on the same host is a data-loss signal. When the same endpoint produces both within a short window, it is a confirmed compromised endpoint that is also moving sensitive data out.

Why this detection works
Correlating an endpoint-security/EDR compromise alert and a DLP exfiltration alert on the same normalized host name confirms, across two independent telemetry domains, that a breach and data loss are occurring together — something neither alert proves alone.

False positives
Very low: requires two independent detection classes on the same host. A benign host that coincidentally has a low-severity DLP event and an unrelated behavioral block; the shared syslog-collector host name is excluded.

Tuning
Exclude verified administration/test hosts; raise the required compromise or DLP alert count for higher confidence; the collector host name is already excluded.

Required telemetry
The endpoint-security/EDR compromise alerts and the DLP exfiltration alerts, joined on the normalized short host name (Kaspersky device, Windows/Defender host, Forcepoint endpoint host).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. norm_host = the compromised endpoint; review compromise_detections and dlp_detections in the alert.
2. Treat as a confirmed compromised endpoint with active data loss — isolate the host, preserve evidence, and begin incident response and data-breach handling.
3. Identify the user(s) and the data moved (DLP files/destination); involve fraud/compliance.
false_positives: Very low: requires two independent detection classes on the same host. A benign host that coincidentally has a low-severity DLP event and an unrelated behavioral block; the shared syslog-collector host name is excluded.
query:
FROM .alerts-security.alerts-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE kibana.alert.rule.name IN ("Kaspersky — Malware or Malicious Object Detected on an Endpoint", "Kaspersky — Behavioral Threat Blocked (Adaptive Anomaly Control)", "Kaspersky — Network Attack Detected Against an Endpoint", "Kaspersky — Multiple Threat Detections on One Endpoint", "Defender — High-Confidence Endpoint/Identity/Office Attack Alert", "Defender — Endpoint Incident Spanning Multiple Attack Tactics", "Defender — New Host Exhibiting Malware or Hacktool Activity", "Defender — User Flagged by Multiple Defender Products", "Windows — UAC Bypass via Auto-Elevated LOLBin", "Windows — Inhibit System Recovery (Ransomware Precursor)", "Windows — Registry Persistence: IFEO / Winlogon / AppInit", "Windows — Scheduled Task Created with Suspicious Action", "AD — Kerberoasting: RC4 Service Ticket Requested", "AD — Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink Modified)", "AD — SPN Added by Non-Computer Principal (Kerberoast Setup)", "AD — Object Security Descriptor Modified (DACL Backdoor)", "AD — Member Added to a Privileged (Tier-0) Group", "AD — KRBTGT Account Password Reset (Golden Ticket Prep / Remediation)", "Forcepoint DLP — Bulk Sensitive Data to Personal / Public Email by One User", "Forcepoint DLP — Sensitive Data Transfer Outside Working Hours", "Forcepoint DLP — Sensitive Data Sent to a Personal / Public Email Domain", "Forcepoint DLP — Cardholder / PCI Data Transfer")
| EVAL norm_host = TO_LOWER(COALESCE(destination.domain, host.name))
| WHERE norm_host IS NOT NULL AND norm_host != "" AND NOT norm_host LIKE "jcb-agent*"
| EVAL is_dlp = kibana.alert.rule.name IN ("Forcepoint DLP — Bulk Sensitive Data to Personal / Public Email by One User", "Forcepoint DLP — Sensitive Data Transfer Outside Working Hours", "Forcepoint DLP — Sensitive Data Sent to a Personal / Public Email Domain", "Forcepoint DLP — Cardholder / PCI Data Transfer")
| STATS compromise_alerts = COUNT(CASE(NOT is_dlp, kibana.alert.rule.name, null)), dlp_alerts = COUNT(CASE(is_dlp, kibana.alert.rule.name, null)), compromise_detections = VALUES(CASE(NOT is_dlp, kibana.alert.rule.name, null)), dlp_detections = VALUES(CASE(is_dlp, kibana.alert.rule.name, null)), users = VALUES(user.name), first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp) BY norm_host
| WHERE compromise_alerts >= 1 AND dlp_alerts >= 1

name: Correlation — Defender + Native Detection on the Same Host
description:
Attacker objective
Compromise a host — Microsoft Defender detects malware, exploitation or suspicious behaviour on the device while the JCB Windows analytics independently detect an attack technique (credential dumping, persistence, lateral execution, ransomware behaviour) on the same host.

Attack logic
A single host independently flagged by Microsoft Defender and by a JCB-native Windows detection within a short window is a corroborated endpoint compromise — for example a Defender malware/exploitation alert alongside native service creation, LSASS dumping or WMI/WinRM execution on the same device.

Why this detection works
Correlating a Defender-sourced alert and a native JCB detection on the same host over the alert stream confirms endpoint compromise across two independent telemetry sources, joined on the device name.

False positives
A busy administration/test host that legitimately trips both sources.

Tuning
Exclude verified administration/test hosts; require a specific high-value native technique if noisy.

Required telemetry
The Defender detection alerts (host.name, derived from the device) and the JCB Windows detection alerts (host.name).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. The host was flagged by both Microsoft Defender and a native Windows detection — review both.
2. This is corroborated endpoint compromise — isolate the host, rotate credentials used on it, and begin IR.
3. Correlate the involved user(s) and reconstruct the timeline from both sources.
false_positives: A busy administration/test host that legitimately trips both sources.

name: Correlation — Defender + Native Detection on the Same User
description:
Attacker objective
Compromise an identity and use it — Microsoft Defender detects the identity/endpoint activity while the JCB Windows/AD analytics independently detect the same account performing an attack technique (Kerberoasting, DCSync, privileged-group change, credential dumping, and similar).

A single account that is independently flagged by Microsoft Defender and by a JCB-native Active Directory/Windows detection within a short window is exhibiting corroborated malicious behaviour — for example a Defender identity alert alongside a Kerberoasting, DCSync or Tier-0 group change by the same user.

Why this detection works
Correlating a Defender-sourced alert and a native JCB detection on the same user over the alert stream confirms account compromise that either source alone cannot, and joins the two telemetry domains on the reliable user identity.

A shared/service account whose legitimate activity independently trips both domains; an authorised scanner identity (excluded).

Tuning
Exclude verified shared/service and scanner accounts; require a specific high-value native technique if noisy.

Required telemetry
The Defender detection alerts (user.name) and the JCB Windows/AD detection alerts (user.name).
author: raadabujaish
note:

name: Correlation — Endpoint Kill Chain: Credential Access then Lateral/Impact
description:
Attacker objective
Progress through the intrusion lifecycle on one host — obtain credentials or enumerate the domain, then use them to move laterally, escalate, persist, or cause impact.

Attack logic
A single high-fidelity detection may be an isolated event. The same host producing a credential-access/discovery detection and a lateral-movement/impact/persistence detection is executing an ordered attack chain.

Why this detection works
Correlating the two attack stages per host over the alert stream confirms progression that either alert alone cannot, with very low false-positive risk because two independent high-fidelity detections must coincide.

False positives
Very low — requires two independent high-fidelity detections on the same host. A busy administration host running multiple sanctioned tools could co-trigger.

Tuning
Exclude verified administration/jump hosts that legitimately trigger both stages; investigate every other host.

Required telemetry
The JCB Windows/AD detection alerts (host.name populated).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. host.name is the compromised endpoint; the detections list shows the credential-access step and the follow-on step.
2. This is a confirmed multi-stage intrusion — isolate the host, rotate credentials used on it, and begin IR immediately.
3. Pivot to the source of the initial access and any accounts whose credentials were exposed.
false_positives: Very low — requires two independent high-fidelity detections on the same host. A busy administration host running multiple sanctioned tools could co-trigger.

FROM .alerts-security.alerts-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE host.name IS NOT NULL AND kibana.alert.rule.name IN ("Windows — LSASS Memory Dump via Known Credential-Theft Tooling", "Windows — Credential Theft: Registry Hive or NTDS.dit Extraction", "Windows — Malicious PowerShell: AMSI/ETW Bypass or Offensive Tooling", "Windows — Pass-the-Hash / Overpass-the-Hash Logon Pattern", "Windows — Ingress Tool Transfer via LOLBin", "Windows — Signed Binary Proxy Execution (LOLBin)", "Windows — UAC Bypass via Auto-Elevated LOLBin", "AD — DCSync: Directory Replication by an Unexpected Principal", "AD — Kerberoasting: RC4 Service Ticket Requested", "AD — AS-REP Roasting: TGT Requested for a Pre-Auth-Disabled Account", "AD — Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink Modified)", "AD — SPN Added by Non-Computer Principal (Kerberoast Setup)", "AD — Domain Reconnaissance via LOLBins / BloodHound", "Windows — Remote Execution via WMI or WinRM", "Windows — Service Installed with Suspicious Image Path", "Windows — Inhibit System Recovery (Ransomware Precursor)", "Windows — Defender / EDR / Firewall Tampering", "Windows — Registry Persistence: IFEO / Winlogon / AppInit", "Windows — Scheduled Task Created with Suspicious Action", "AD — Member Added to a Privileged (Tier-0) Group", "AD — Object Security Descriptor Modified (DACL Backdoor)", "AD — Group Policy Object Modified by an Unexpected Principal", "AD — KRBTGT Account Password Reset (Golden Ticket Prep / Remediation)")
| EVAL stage = CASE(kibana.alert.rule.name IN ("Windows — LSASS Memory Dump via Known Credential-Theft Tooling", "Windows — Credential Theft: Registry Hive or NTDS.dit Extraction", "Windows — Malicious PowerShell: AMSI/ETW Bypass or Offensive Tooling", "Windows — Pass-the-Hash / Overpass-the-Hash Logon Pattern", "Windows — Ingress Tool Transfer via LOLBin", "Windows — Signed Binary Proxy Execution (LOLBin)", "Windows — UAC Bypass via Auto-Elevated LOLBin", "AD — DCSync: Directory Replication by an Unexpected Principal", "AD — Kerberoasting: RC4 Service Ticket Requested", "AD — AS-REP Roasting: TGT Requested for a Pre-Auth-Disabled Account", "AD — Shadow Credentials (msDS-KeyCredentialLink Modified)", "AD — SPN Added by Non-Computer Principal (Kerberoast Setup)", "AD — Domain Reconnaissance via LOLBins / BloodHound"), "1-credential-access/discovery", "2-lateral/impact/persistence")

name: Correlation — External Source Attacking Multiple Security Layers
description:
Attacker objective
Compromise the bank by attacking across multiple perimeter layers — the web-application firewall, the next-gen firewall IPS, and the edge firewall — from a single source.

Attack logic
An opportunistic scan hits one layer. A source that trips detections on two or more distinct perimeter products (WAF, FortiGate IPS, PAN-OS) is running a deliberate, multi-vector campaign against the institution.

Why this detection works
Correlating distinct perimeter product families per external source over the alert stream elevates coordinated cross-layer attacks above isolated single-layer noise.

False positives
A shared NAT/proxy egress aggregating many clients; an authorized external penetration test.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned testers and known shared egress IPs; raise the distinct-layer threshold for higher confidence.

Required telemetry
The perimeter/WAF detection alerts (F5, FortiGate, PAN-OS) with source.ip populated.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. source.ip is the external attacker; review which layers and detections it triggered.
2. Treat as a targeted campaign: block the source at the edge and hunt for any successful reach to internal assets.
false_positives: A shared NAT/proxy egress aggregating many clients; an authorized external penetration test.
query:
FROM .alerts-security.alerts-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE source.ip IS NOT NULL AND (kibana.alert.rule.name LIKE "F5 WAF*" OR kibana.alert.rule.name LIKE "FortiGate*" OR kibana.alert.rule.name LIKE "PAN-OS*")
| EVAL product = CASE(kibana.alert.rule.name LIKE "F5 WAF*", "F5-WAF", kibana.alert.rule.name LIKE "PAN-OS*", "PAN-OS", "FortiGate")
| STATS layers = COUNT_DISTINCT(product), products = VALUES(product), detections = VALUES(kibana.alert.rule.name), alerts = COUNT() BY source.ip
| WHERE layers >= 2

name: Correlation — Host Exhibiting Multiple Distinct Attack Behaviors
description:
Attacker objective
Operate extensively on a single compromised host, leaving traces across several distinct attack techniques.

Attack logic
The more distinct high-fidelity techniques a single host exhibits in a short window, the higher the certainty of an active, hands-on-keyboard compromise rather than an isolated anomaly.

Why this detection works
Counting distinct high-fidelity JCB endpoint detections per host over the alert stream surfaces heavily-active hosts as a single, top-priority alert.

False positives
Very low — requires three independent high-fidelity detections on one host. A heavily-used administration host is the main candidate for tuning.

Tuning
Exclude verified administration hosts; lower or raise the distinct-detection threshold to fit the environment.

Required telemetry
The JCB Windows/AD detection alerts (host.name populated).
author: raadabujaish

## Investigation guide
1. host.name is the compromised endpoint; review the full list of distinct detections it produced.
2. Treat as a high-confidence active intrusion — isolate, preserve evidence and begin IR.
3. Reconstruct the timeline from the individual detections to scope the incident.
false_positives: Very low — requires three independent high-fidelity detections on one host. A heavily-used administration host is the main candidate for tuning.

name: Correlation — Malware-Infected Endpoint Communicating with External C2
description:
Attacker objective
