description: This rule detects an anomalously high volume of traffic originating from a Multiple source IP address targeting a specific Service. A large number of requests in a short period can indicate an attempt For a DDoS attack, rendering it unavailable for legitimate traffic.

name: Brute Force - O365 Failed Logins
description: Triggers when an IP address fails to log in to O365 more than 10 times within 5 minutes.
author: Anas - Scanwave
note:
1. Check if the source IP has multiple failed logins for different accounts.
2. Verify if the IP is associated with known attackers (threat intelligence lookup).
3. Check if any successful login follows the failed attempts.
4. Correlate with firewall or endpoint logs to see if other suspicious activity exists.
5. If necessary, block the IP and reset compromised accounts.
false_positives: Service accounts attempting to authenticate automatically.
Failed logins due to expired passwords.
Users with mistyped passwords multiple times.
query: event.action:"UserLoginFailed" and o365.audit.ActorIpAddress:* and not o365.audit.LogonError:"DeviceAuthenticationFailed"

name: Entra ID — Application Credential (Secret or Certificate) Added
description:
Attacker objective
Establish stealthy, long-lived access to the tenant by adding a client secret or certificate to an application or service principal, then authenticating as that application.

Attack logic
Adding credentials to an app registration or service principal lets an attacker obtain tokens as that application — a common cloud persistence and privilege-abuse technique that survives user password resets and MFA.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records certificate/secret additions to applications with the target application and the acting principal; the operation is low-volume and security-relevant.

False positives
A legitimate administrator or DevOps process rotating an application secret; an onboarded integration (e.g. a SIEM connector).

Tuning
Allowlist verified integration applications and rotation automation; alert on credentials added to unexpected apps or by unexpected actors.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 8, Operation 'Update/Create application – Certificates and secrets management' (ModifiedProperties.KeyDescription, ObjectId=Application, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. ObjectId identifies the application; ModifiedProperties.KeyDescription shows the added credential; user.name is the actor.
2. Confirm the credential addition was authorised change; if not, remove the credential and review the application's granted permissions and recent token activity.
false_positives: A legitimate administrator or DevOps process rotating an application secret; an onboarded integration (e.g. a SIEM connector).
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:("*Certificates and secrets management*")

name: Entra ID — Member Added to a Privileged Directory Role
description:
Attacker objective
Escalate to tenant-wide control by adding an account to a highly-privileged Entra ID (Azure AD) directory role such as Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator or Application Administrator.

Attack logic
Directory-role membership changes to privileged roles are rare and grant far-reaching control over identities, applications and data. An addition to these roles is among the most consequential cloud identity changes.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records role additions with the target role display name and the acting principal; scoping to the privileged role set makes any such grant a high-signal event.

False positives
Authorised administration or a planned role assignment.

Tuning
Correlate with change tickets; allowlist verified break-glass/administration workflows; treat Global Administrator additions as highest priority.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 8 / AzureActiveDirectory, Operation 'Add member to role.' (ModifiedProperties.Role_DisplayName, ObjectId=target, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. ObjectId is the account added; Role_DisplayName is the role granted; user.name is the actor.
2. Verify authorisation; if unauthorised, remove the role, disable the account and investigate the actor and their recent sign-ins.
3. Review what the newly-privileged account did next.
false_positives: Authorised administration or a planned role assignment.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:"Add member to role." and o365.audit.ModifiedProperties.Role_DisplayName.NewValue:("Global Administrator" or "Privileged Role Administrator" or "Privileged Authentication Administrator" or "Application Administrator" or "Cloud Application Administrator" or "Exchange Administrator" or "SharePoint Administrator" or "Security Administrator" or "User Administrator" or "Conditional Access Administrator" or "Hybrid Identity Administrator" or "Intune Administrator" or "Authentication Administrator" or "Domain Name Administrator" or "Helpdesk Administrator")

name: Entra ID — OAuth Consent, Permission Grant or Service Principal Added
description:
Attacker objective
Gain persistent, MFA-resistant access to mailboxes, files or the directory by consenting to a malicious OAuth application or granting it API permissions (illicit consent / service-principal abuse).

Attack logic
Attackers register or reuse an application and obtain consent or a permission grant (for example to Microsoft Graph Mail.Read/Files.ReadWrite.All), then access data as the application. Adding a service principal or app-role assignment extends the same abuse.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records consent events, delegated-permission grants, app-role assignments and service-principal additions with the target application and the acting principal.

False positives
Legitimate application onboarding and admin consent for sanctioned SaaS/integration apps.

Tuning
Allowlist verified applications; prioritise user-consent (non-admin) events and grants of high-risk Graph permissions; review the application publisher.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 8, Operations 'Consent to application.', 'Add delegated permission grant.', 'Add app role assignment to service principal.', 'Add service principal.' (Target=application, ModifiedProperties, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the application (Target/ObjectId) and the permissions granted; confirm the app is sanctioned.
2. For an unknown app, revoke the consent/grant and service principal, and review what data the app accessed.
3. Check whether the consent was user- or admin-granted and by whom.
false_positives: Legitimate application onboarding and admin consent for sanctioned SaaS/integration apps.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:("Consent to application." or "Add delegated permission grant." or "Add app role assignment to service principal." or "Add service principal.")

name: Exchange Online — Mailbox External Forwarding Configured
description:
Attacker objective
Silently exfiltrate a target's email by configuring mailbox-level forwarding to an attacker-controlled address — a hallmark of business email compromise (BEC).

Attack logic
Setting ForwardingSmtpAddress or ForwardingAddress on a mailbox copies inbound mail to another address. Attackers use this after account takeover to monitor a victim's communications and intercept financial correspondence.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records Set-Mailbox operations with the forwarding parameters and the acting principal; mailbox-level forwarding changes are infrequent and high-signal.

False positives
A legitimate administrator configuring forwarding for a departed employee or a shared/role mailbox.

Tuning
Confirm the forwarding target is internal and authorised; treat forwarding to an external domain as high priority; allowlist sanctioned mail-routing changes.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 1 / Exchange, Operation 'Set-Mailbox' (Parameters.ForwardingSmtpAddress / ForwardingAddress, ObjectId=mailbox, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the mailbox (ObjectId) and the forwarding target; determine whether the target is external.
2. If unauthorised, remove the forwarding, reset the mailbox owner's credentials, and investigate the account for takeover (sign-ins, inbox rules, consent grants).
false_positives: A legitimate administrator configuring forwarding for a departed employee or a shared/role mailbox.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:"Set-Mailbox" and (o365.audit.Parameters.ForwardingSmtpAddress:* or o365.audit.Parameters.ForwardingAddress:*)

name: Exchange Online — Mailbox FullAccess or SendAs Delegation Granted
description:
Attacker objective
Gain persistent access to another user's mailbox, or the ability to send as them, by granting FullAccess or SendAs delegation — used for BEC, data theft and impersonation.

Attack logic
FullAccess lets a principal read an entire mailbox; SendAs lets them send mail as the mailbox owner. Attackers grant these to a controlled account to persist access and impersonate staff after a compromise.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records mailbox-permission and recipient-permission grants with the grantee, access right and acting principal; excluding built-in service/role assignees isolates human-driven delegation.

False positives
Legitimate delegation for shared mailboxes, assistants or team mailboxes.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned shared-mailbox delegation; prioritise FullAccess/SendAs granted to individual user accounts; correlate with the grantee's activity.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 1, Operations 'Add-MailboxPermission' (FullAccess) / 'Add-RecipientPermission' (SendAs) (Parameters.User=grantee, ObjectId=mailbox, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the mailbox, the grantee (Parameters.User) and the access right; confirm the delegation is authorised.
2. If unauthorised, remove the permission and investigate both the actor and the grantee for compromise.
false_positives: Legitimate delegation for shared mailboxes, assistants or team mailboxes.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:("Add-MailboxPermission" or "Add-RecipientPermission") and not o365.audit.Parameters.User:("Discovery Management" or "Organization Management" or "Exchange Servers" or "NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM")

name: Exchange Online — Transport (Mail Flow) Rule Created or Modified
description:
Attacker objective
Intercept, redirect, copy or silently drop organisational email by creating or modifying an Exchange transport (mail-flow) rule.

Attack logic
Transport rules act on all mail flow. An attacker can add a rule that blind-copies mail to an external address, redirects specific messages, or deletes security-related notifications to hide activity.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records transport-rule create/modify/remove operations with the acting principal; these are infrequent administrative changes.

False positives
A legitimate mail-administration change to routing, disclaimers or compliance rules.

Tuning
Correlate with change control; review the rule's actions (bcc/redirect/delete) and conditions; allowlist sanctioned mail-admin automation.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 1, Operations 'New-TransportRule' / 'Set-TransportRule' / 'Remove-TransportRule' (Parameters, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Review the transport rule's conditions and actions (especially blind-copy, redirect or delete).
2. Confirm the change was authorised; a rule that exfiltrates or drops mail is high-risk — revert and investigate the actor.
false_positives: A legitimate mail-administration change to routing, disclaimers or compliance rules.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:("New-TransportRule" or "Set-TransportRule" or "Remove-TransportRule")

name: Microsoft Teams — Application Installed
description:
Attacker objective
Deliver a malicious application into the collaboration platform — a Teams app can request permissions, phish users, or exfiltrate messages and files.

Attack logic
Attackers publish or side-load a malicious Teams app to gain a foothold in the collaboration environment. A newly-seen app being installed warrants review of its publisher and permissions.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records Teams app installations; a new-terms model over the app identity surfaces first-seen applications while suppressing the routine re-installation of already-known apps.

False positives
Onboarding of a legitimate, sanctioned Teams application.

Tuning
Allowlist approved apps; review the publisher and requested permissions of any new app.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 25 / MicrosoftTeams, Operation 'AppInstalled' (AddOnName/app identity, user.name).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the installed application and its publisher; confirm it is sanctioned.
2. If untrusted, remove the app and review what it accessed and which users it reached.
false_positives: Onboarding of a legitimate, sanctioned Teams application.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:"AppInstalled"

name: O365 DLP — High Endpoint DLP Volume by One User (Daily Aggregate)
description: Replaces per-event Purview DLP promotion (71k alerts/7d) with one daily aggregate per heavy user: ≥50 endpoint DLP events in 24h, with action breakdown. Suppression per user per day. Extended to include Exchange DLP policy matches (393/7d measured) so disabling the per-event Purview promotion loses no channel.
author: JCB Detection Engineering
query: FROM logs-o365.audit-* METADATA _id, _index, _version | WHERE event.code IN ("DLPEndpoint","ComplianceDLPExchange") | STATS dlp_events = COUNT(), actions = VALUES(event.action), channels = VALUES(event.code) BY user.name | WHERE dlp_events >= 200

name: O365 — MFA Fatigue: Repeated MFA Challenges Rejected/Ignored for One User
description: ≥5 UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequiredInterrupt failures for one account within the window — the MFA push-bombing pattern. Baseline: max 10 such events per user per WEEK (measured), so this stays quiet until a real fatigue attack. Attack-shaped watcher, not noise.
author: JCB Detection Engineering
query: event.action:"UserLoginFailed" and o365.audit.LogonError:"UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequiredInterrupt"

name: O365 — Password Spraying: One Source Failing Against Many Accounts
description: One source IP with failed logins against ≥8 distinct O365 accounts in 45 minutes, excluding the bank egress NAT (94.249.88.0/24 — internal users all appear from it). timestamp_override handles the o365 API ingest lag that blinded earlier rules.
author: JCB Detection Engineering
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:"UserLoginFailed" and not source.ip:"94.249.88.0/24"

name: Office 365 -  Changes
description: This rule monitors Office 365 audit activity for any changes made to user or account properties. Such updates may include adjustments to authentication methods, security settings, or account attributes. While these actions can be part of normal administration, unexpected or unauthorized modifications could indicate attempts to weaken security controls or gain unauthorized access. This rule provides visibility into all account property changes so they can be reviewed and validated.
query: o365.audit.ModifiedProperties:*

name: Office 365 - MFA Enable/Disable
description: Detects when strong authentication is enabled or disabled, as these changes may impact account security.

name: QA - Office 365 High Severity
description: Office 365 - High Severity

name: QA - Office 365  Medium Severity
description: Office 365 - Medium Severity

name: SharePoint/OneDrive — Burst of Anonymous Sharing Links by a User
description:
Attacker objective
Expose or exfiltrate sensitive documents by creating many anonymous ('anyone with the link') sharing links, which require no authentication to access.

Attack logic
Anonymous links bypass tenant access controls. A user creating them in bulk within a short window is mass-exposing data, whether as a malicious insider or a compromised account.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records anonymous-link creation per user; a per-user burst distinguishes mass exposure from the routine single-link sharing that makes per-event alerting unusable.

False positives
A user legitimately publishing many documents for external collaboration.

Tuning
Set the per-user burst threshold above the routine sharing rate; allowlist sanctioned external-collaboration accounts; review the shared sites/files.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 14 / SharePointSharing, Operation 'AnonymousLinkCreated' (SiteUrl, user.name).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Review the sites/files the user shared anonymously and whether they are sensitive.
2. Confirm business justification; if none, revoke the links and investigate the account for compromise or insider data theft.
false_positives: A user legitimately publishing many documents for external collaboration.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:"AnonymousLinkCreated"

name: SharePoint — Site Collection Administrator Added
description:
Attacker objective
Gain full control of a SharePoint site collection — including all its documents — by adding an account as a site collection administrator.

Attack logic
Site collection administrators can access and export all content in a site. Adding one is a privilege change that can precede bulk data access or exfiltration.

Why this detection works
The unified audit log records site-collection-admin additions with the target site, the added account and the acting principal; the operation is infrequent.

False positives
Legitimate SharePoint administration or site-ownership changes.

Tuning
Correlate with change control; prioritise additions to sensitive sites and additions of unexpected accounts.

Required telemetry
o365.audit RecordType 14, Operation 'SiteCollectionAdminAdded' (SiteUrl, target, user.name=actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the site and the added administrator; confirm the change is authorised.
2. If unauthorised, remove the admin and review the site for bulk access/download of its content.
false_positives: Legitimate SharePoint administration or site-ownership changes.
query: event.dataset:"o365.audit" and event.action:"SiteCollectionAdminAdded"

name: Oracle — CREATE TABLE by Unexpected Principal
description:
Attacker objective
Stage sensitive data for theft by copying tables (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) before exfiltration.

Attack logic
CTAS in production is normally an ETL operation by a known service account. CREATE TABLE by any other principal — especially copying client or account tables — is data-staging behaviour.

Why this detection works
Unified Audit records the statement and principal, so allowlisting ETL makes other CTAS a high-signal event.

False positives
A new ETL/reporting account.

Tuning
Allowlist verified accounts; review the CTAS source table for sensitivity.

Required telemetry
Oracle Unified Audit shipped as apps-* (ACTION_NAME, USERNAME, SQL_TEXT).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SQL_TEXT shows the CTAS source; copying sensitive client/account tables by an unexpected actor is data-staging for theft.
2. Correlate with any subsequent DB-link creation or large outbound transfer from the DB host.
false_positives: A new ETL/reporting account.
query: ACTION_NAME.keyword:"CREATE TABLE" and not USERNAME.keyword:"INH_LIFE"

name: Oracle — Dangerous ALTER SYSTEM Command
description:
Attacker objective
Weaken database security (disable auditing, change security parameters) or cause disruption via ALTER SYSTEM.

Attack logic
Routine ALTER SYSTEM in production is almost entirely session management (for example KILL SESSION) performed by a known service account. An ALTER SYSTEM that is not a kill-session, or is issued by a different principal, may be a parameter or security change.

Why this detection works
Unified Audit records the full statement text and the acting principal, so filtering out the routine session-management pattern isolates security-relevant ALTER SYSTEM.

False positives
A DBA legitimately changing a parameter during a maintenance window.

Tuning
Review SQL_TEXT; allowlist specific approved parameter changes or maintenance windows.

Required telemetry
Oracle Unified Audit shipped as apps-* (ACTION_NAME, USERNAME, SQL_TEXT.keyword).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SQL_TEXT shows the exact command; a non-session-management ALTER SYSTEM (e.g. SET audit_trail, security params) is the concern.
2. Confirm change control and DBA authorisation.
false_positives: A DBA legitimately changing a parameter during a maintenance window.
query: ACTION_NAME.keyword:"ALTER SYSTEM" and (not USERNAME.keyword:"INH_LIFE" or (not SQL_TEXT.keyword:*KILL* and not SQL_TEXT.keyword:*kill*))

name: Oracle — Database Link Created by Unexpected Principal
description:
Attacker objective
Create a database link to an attacker-controlled or external database to exfiltrate banking data, or to pivot between systems.

Attack logic
Database links are an integration feature normally created by a known service account and pointed at known internal databases. A link created by any other principal, or one that points at an external/unknown host, is a potential exfiltration or pivot channel.

Why this detection works
Unified Audit records CREATE DATABASE LINK with the principal and statement text, so allowlisting the integration account and reviewing the target host turns link creation into a high-signal event.

False positives
A new legitimate integration account.

Tuning
Allowlist verified integration accounts; additionally review the USING clause (target host) for external addresses.

Required telemetry
Oracle Unified Audit shipped as apps-* (ACTION_NAME, USERNAME, SQL_TEXT).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SQL_TEXT contains the link name and USING (target host); external or unknown targets indicate a likely exfiltration channel.
2. Drop the link if unauthorised and investigate the creating principal.
false_positives: A new legitimate integration account.
query: ACTION_NAME.keyword:"CREATE PUBLIC DATABASE LINK" and not USERNAME.keyword:"INH_LIFE"

name: Oracle DB — Database User Altered (Password/Privilege Change)
description: Detects ALTER USER operations on Oracle accounts (password reset, account unlock, privilege/profile change) — used for account takeover or persistence.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SQL_TEXT` shows what changed (IDENTIFIED BY = password change; ACCOUNT UNLOCK; GRANT).
2. Focus on changes to privileged accounts.
## Response
Reverse unauthorised changes; investigate.
author: raadabujaish
query: ACTION_NAME:"ALTER USER"

name: Oracle — DELETE by Unexpected Principal
description:
Attacker objective
Destroy banking records, or delete audit rows to cover tracks (anti-forensics), using SQL DELETE.

Attack logic
In a healthy core-banking database, DELETE activity is dominated by a small, fixed set of automated maintenance statements run by known service accounts. Interactive users and unknown principals do not routinely issue DELETE against banking or audit tables. The rule allowlists the sanctioned DELETE service accounts and alerts on DELETE by any other principal.

Why this detection works
Database Unified Audit records the action name and the acting principal for every statement, so an allowlist of sanctioned DELETE accounts turns any out-of-baseline DELETE into a single, high-signal event.

False positives
A newly introduced legitimate batch/service account that performs DELETE before it is added to the allowlist.

Tuning
Maintain the service-account allowlist and add verified batch/ETL accounts after change control. Optionally scope by target schema to also catch a sanctioned account deleting from an unexpected (production) table.

Required telemetry
Oracle Unified Audit shipped as apps-* (ACTION_NAME, USERNAME/.keyword, SQL_TEXT).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the principal (USERNAME) and the target object (SQL_TEXT).
2. A DELETE against production banking or audit tables by a human or unknown account is high-risk.
3. Correlate with the account's session and prior activity; contain the account if unauthorised.
false_positives: A newly introduced legitimate batch/service account that performs DELETE before it is added to the allowlist.
query: ACTION_NAME.keyword:"DELETE" and not USERNAME.keyword:("BANKSYS" or "JCB_AML" or "BANKSBPM")

name: Oracle — New Principal Performing a Privileged Operation
description:
Attacker objective
A compromised or newly-created account begins performing privileged database operations (valid-account misuse / insider abuse).

Attack logic
Privileged database actions are performed by a small, stable set of service and admin accounts. The first time a principal not seen in the historical window performs a privileged action is a behavioural anomaly that complements the per-action rules.

Why this detection works
A new-terms model over the acting principal auto-baselines the known set from history and fires only on a genuinely new privileged actor.

False positives
Onboarding of a new legitimate service/admin account.

Tuning
Verify and allowlist new accounts; the history window auto-baselines over time.

Required telemetry
Oracle Unified Audit shipped as apps-* (ACTION_NAME, USERNAME).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the new principal and the privileged action performed.
2. Confirm whether the account was legitimately onboarded; if not, contain and investigate.
false_positives: Onboarding of a new legitimate service/admin account.
query: ACTION_NAME.keyword:("DELETE" or "TRUNCATE TABLE" or "ALTER SYSTEM" or "CREATE PUBLIC DATABASE LINK" or "CREATE TABLE" or "PL/SQL EXECUTE" or "CREATE USER" or "DROP TABLE")

name: Oracle — TRUNCATE TABLE by Unexpected Principal
description:
Attacker objective
Irrecoverably destroy data in banking tables. TRUNCATE is fast, minimally logged, and cannot be rolled back.

Attack logic
TRUNCATE in a core-banking database is normally limited to ETL/staging refreshes performed by a known service account against a fixed set of staging tables. TRUNCATE by any other principal is outside that pattern.

Why this detection works
Unified Audit captures the action and principal for every statement, so allowlisting the ETL account makes any other TRUNCATE a high-signal event.

False positives
A new ETL/maintenance service account not yet allowlisted.

Tuning
Allowlist verified ETL accounts. To also catch the ETL account truncating a production (non-staging) table, add an object allowlist scoped to the sanctioned staging tables.

Required telemetry
Oracle Unified Audit shipped as apps-* (ACTION_NAME, USERNAME, SQL_TEXT).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. SQL_TEXT names the truncated table; confirm it is not a production banking table.
2. Confirm the actor is an authorised ETL principal.
3. If unauthorised, treat as data-destruction and begin IR.
false_positives: A new ETL/maintenance service account not yet allowlisted.
query: ACTION_NAME.keyword:"TRUNCATE TABLE" and not USERNAME.keyword:"INH_LIFE"

name: Core Banking App — Privilege Granted by Unexpected Administrator
description:
Attacker objective
Grant banking application functions/privileges to an attacker-controlled account (privilege escalation / persistence).

Attack logic
Application privilege grants are performed by a small set of authorised administrators. A grant performed by any other administrator identity is outside the sanctioned set.

Why this detection works
The application audit records the granting admin, the recipient and the function granted, so allowlisting sanctioned granters makes any other grant a high-signal event.

False positives
A newly authorised administrator.

Tuning
Allowlist verified admin IDs; review the source address for an unexpected origin.

Required telemetry
Core Application audit (apps-*, type='Core Application'): GRANTED_BY, USER_ID_GRANTED, FUNCTION_NAME, USR_IPADDRESS.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. GRANTED_BY = the granting admin; USER_ID_GRANTED = the recipient; FUNCTION_NAME = the banking function; USR_IPADDRESS = source.
2. Confirm the grant was authorised and the granter is a sanctioned admin.
false_positives: A newly authorised administrator.
query: type.keyword:"Core Application" and not GRANTED_BY.keyword:"3174"

name: PAN-OS — Firewall Configuration Change by an Unexpected Administrator
description:
Attacker objective
A compromised or rogue administrator modifies the perimeter firewall — adding an allow rule, weakening a policy, or manipulating admin accounts — to enable access or evade defenses.

Attack logic
Firewall configuration is performed by a small, stable set of administrators. A configuration change by an administrator not seen in the historical window is anomalous on an internet-edge firewall.

Why this detection works
PAN-OS CONFIG logs fully attribute each change to an admin; a new-terms model auto-baselines the known admin set and fires on a genuinely new one.

False positives
Onboarding of a new legitimate firewall admin.

Tuning
Allowlist verified new admins; the history window auto-baselines over time.

Required telemetry
PAN-OS CONFIG logs (admin, cmd, path, result).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. admin = the account; path/cmd = what changed (watch for security rulebase and management-user changes).
2. Confirm the admin was authorised and review the specific change against change control.
false_positives: Onboarding of a new legitimate firewall admin.
query: panw.panos.type:"CONFIG"

name: PAN-OS — Genuine Exploitation Attempt (non-informational)
description:
Attacker objective
Exploit an edge or internet-facing service (RCE, buffer overflow, brute-force, DoS).

Attack logic
Edge threat logs are dominated by benign informational signatures (for example TLS-detection events). Scoping to genuine exploit threat categories (code-execution, overflow, brute-force, DoS) isolates real exploitation attempts.

Why this detection works
Filtering on exploit threat categories removes the large informational-signature noise class.

False positives
An authorised scanner; internal service brute-force false-positives.

Tuning
Exclude sanctioned scanners; review the threat name and target exposure.

Required telemetry
PAN-OS THREAT logs (sub_type:vulnerability, threat_category, threat name, source.ip).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. threat name/category + source.ip: confirm the exploit and whether the target is internet-facing.
2. Escalate genuine exploitation of an exposed asset.
false_positives: An authorised scanner; internal service brute-force false-positives.
query: panw.panos.sub_type:"vulnerability" and panw.panos.threat_category:("code-execution" or "overflow" or "brute-force" or "dos")

name: PAN-OS — High-Severity Threat Allowed Through the Perimeter
description: Promotes only actionable Palo Alto threat events: high/critical IPS or spyware signatures whose session was ALLOWED (not blocked). Replaces the deleted catch-all External Alerts rule (which promoted 550k+ PAN-OS events/day) with a scoped, low-volume signal for threats that got through.
author: JCB Detection Engineering
query: event.dataset:"panw.panos" and panw.panos.sub_type:(vulnerability or spyware) and panw.panos.action:(alert or allow) and event.severity <= 2

name: PAN-OS — Sensitive Firewall Change (Security Rule or Admin User)
description:
Attacker objective
Weaken the perimeter by adding/modifying/deleting a security policy rule to open access, or by manipulating firewall admin accounts.

Attack logic
Changes to security-rule policy or to firewall management users are the highest-risk configuration operations on an edge firewall. This rule catches such sensitive changes by any administrator, complementing the new-admin rule.

Why this detection works
PAN-OS CONFIG logs fully attribute each change (admin, cmd, path); scoping to security-rule and management-user paths surfaces the sensitive subset.

False positives
Routine authorised rule/user maintenance.

Tuning
Operate as a review queue and correlate with change tickets; optionally exclude routine automation identities.

Required telemetry
PAN-OS CONFIG logs (type, cmd, path, admin).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. admin + path + cmd = who changed which security rule or user.
2. Verify against change control; a rule that opens inbound access, or a newly added admin, is high-risk.
false_positives: Routine authorised rule/user maintenance.
query: panw.panos.type:"CONFIG" and panw.panos.cmd:("delete" or "set" or "edit" or "rename") and (panw.panos.path:*rulebase*security*rules* or panw.panos.path:*mgt-config*users*)

name: SWIFT — Administrative or Attacker Tooling Executed on a SWIFT Server
description:
Attacker objective
Operate hands-on-keyboard on the SWIFT payment platform — running scripting interpreters, remote-execution utilities, credential-dumping or reconnaissance tooling — to stage fraud, dump credentials, or move laterally.

Detection logic
The SWIFT servers run a tightly-scoped set of payment and file-transfer processes. Execution of PowerShell, PsExec/WMIC remote-exec utilities, credential-dumping tools, or reconnaissance binaries on these servers is outside normal operation and indicates interactive attacker activity or malicious automation on a Tier-0 asset.

Why this detection works
Scoping process-creation events on the SWIFT servers to attacker/administrative tooling (excluding the platform's normal command and SFTP processes) surfaces hands-on-keyboard activity on the payment system.

False positives
A sanctioned administrator or vendor running a diagnostic script/tool during an approved maintenance window.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned maintenance tooling/windows; some environments run legitimate PowerShell/scripting in SWIFT automation — baseline and exclude verified scripts; prioritise credential-dumping and remote-exec tooling.

Required telemetry
Windows Security on the SWIFT servers: event.code 4688, process.name/process.executable, process.command_line (if enabled), SubjectUserName, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. process.name/executable = the tool; SubjectUserName = who ran it; host.name = the SWIFT server.
2. Confirm whether an approved maintenance was underway; PowerShell, PsExec, WMIC, procdump or recon tooling on a SWIFT server is high-risk — treat as a suspected intrusion and isolate/preserve.
3. Correlate with the interactive-logon and system-change detections on the same SWIFT server.
false_positives: A sanctioned administrator or vendor running a diagnostic script/tool during an approved maintenance window.
query: (host.name:*sw-app* or host.name:saa* or host.name:*swift*) and event.code:"4688" and process.name:("psexec.exe" or "psexesvc.exe" or "paexec.exe" or "wmic.exe" or "whoami.exe" or "nltest.exe" or "mshta.exe" or "certutil.exe" or "bitsadmin.exe" or "procdump.exe" or "procdump64.exe" or "ntdsutil.exe" or "vssadmin.exe" or "mimikatz.exe" or "rubeus.exe" or "sharphound.exe" or "adfind.exe" or "psloggedon.exe" or "netscan.exe" or "cobaltstrike.exe" or "advanced_port_scanner.exe")

name: SWIFT — New Interactive or Remote Logon to a SWIFT Server
description:
Attacker objective
Gain hands-on access to the SWIFT payment platform by logging on interactively or over RDP with a new or unauthorized account, to view or manipulate international payments.

Detection logic
The SWIFT servers are Tier-0 payment assets accessed interactively by a small, fixed set of administrators and monitoring accounts. An interactive (type 2), RDP (type 10) or unlock (type 7) logon by an account never seen before on the SWIFT estate is a high-risk access event.

Why this detection works
A new-terms model over the interactive/RDP logon account, scoped to the SWIFT servers and excluding known monitoring/system accounts, fires only when a genuinely new operator touches the payment platform.

False positives
Onboarding of a new authorized SWIFT administrator; a new monitoring/service account performing an interactive logon.

Tuning
Allowlist verified new SWIFT administrators after review; keep the monitoring-account exclusions current; treat any unexpected interactive logon to SWIFT as an incident.

Required telemetry
Windows Security on the SWIFT servers: event.code 4624, LogonType 2/7/10, TargetUserName, IpAddress, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. TargetUserName = the new account; host.name = which SWIFT server; IpAddress = source of the logon.
2. Confirm the account is an authorized SWIFT operator/admin and the access was expected; an unexpected interactive logon to SWIFT is a suspected fraud/intrusion event — escalate.
3. Review what the session did (process execution, config/system changes) on the SWIFT server.
false_positives: Onboarding of a new authorized SWIFT administrator; a new monitoring/service account performing an interactive logon.
query: (host.name:*sw-app* or host.name:saa* or host.name:*swift*) and event.code:"4624" and winlog.event_data.LogonType:("2" or "7" or "10") and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:("SolarWinds" or "NCM" or "*$" or "DWM-*" or "UMFD-*" or "SYSTEM")

name: SWIFT — Unauthorized System Change on the SWIFT Payment Server
description:
Attacker objective
Tamper with the SWIFT payment server — install a service, create/enable a local account, add an account to a privileged group, or clear the security log — to establish persistence or fraudulently manipulate international payments.

Attack logic
The SWIFT application server is a Tier-0 payment asset; any OS-level change to it (new service, new/enabled account, privileged-group addition, log clearing) outside authorized change control is high-risk and can enable payment fraud or hide it.

Why this detection works
Scoping Windows service-installation, account-management, privileged-group and log-clear events to the SWIFT server surfaces integrity-affecting changes to the payment platform; these events are rare or zero on this server in normal operation.

False positives
An authorized, change-controlled maintenance action on the SWIFT server.

Tuning
Allowlist scheduled maintenance windows and sanctioned admin service/account changes; correlate every hit with the change-management record; treat any log-clear (1102) or new privileged account as an incident until proven authorized.

Required telemetry
Windows Security on the SWIFT server: event.code 4697/7045 (service), 4720/4722/4738 (account), 4728/4732/4756 (group), 1102 (log cleared), host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. host.name = the SWIFT server; event.code identifies the change (service install, account, group, log clear).
2. Verify against change management; a new service, new privileged account, or a cleared log on the SWIFT server is a suspected integrity/fraud event — escalate immediately.
3. Correlate with the acting account's logons and with any SWIFT application activity in the same window.
false_positives: An authorized, change-controlled maintenance action on the SWIFT server.
query: (host.name:*sw-app* or host.name:saa* or host.name:*swift*) and event.code:("4697" or "7045" or "1102" or "4720" or "4722" or "4732" or "4756" or "4728" or "4738" or "4719" or "4739" or "4964")

name: VMware vSphere — vCenter/ESXi Account Password Changed
description: Detects a password change on a VMware vCenter/ESXi account (e.g. the vpxuser service account or a VIM/local account) on an ESXi host. vSphere is a Tier-0 platform controlling every VM; unexpected credential changes here indicate account takeover or unauthorised administrative change.
note:
## Investigation
1. `message` names the account (e.g. vpxuser) and the ESXi host.
2. vpxuser passwords rotate automatically via vCenter — an out-of-band change to a named admin/root account is the concern.
## Response
Confirm the change was an authorised/automatic rotation; if not, reset the credential and investigate.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"vsphere.log" and message:"password was changed"

name: VMware vSphere — Virtual Machine Created (non-backup)
description: Detects creation of a new virtual machine in vCenter by a non-backup principal (excludes routine Veeam.Backup restores). The message names the actor, the new VM and the target ESXi host. Rogue VM creation can be used to run unmonitored workloads or stage attacks inside the virtualization Tier-0.
note:
## Investigation
1. The `message` contains `[DOMAIN\actor] [Datacenter] [taskid] Creating <VM> on <host>` — identify the actor and confirm the VM against change control.
2. Human-admin VM creation outside a provisioning window is the concern.
## Response
If unauthorised, power off/remove the VM and investigate the actor account.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"vsphere.log" and message:"Creating" and message:"in NBI-Datacenter" and not message:"Veeam.Backup"

name: VMware vSphere — Virtual Machine Deleted (non-backup)
description: Detects removal/deletion of a virtual machine from vCenter by a non-backup principal (excludes routine Veeam.Backup lifecycle). Deleting a VM destroys its workload and data — a destructive/impact action or attacker cleanup on the virtualization Tier-0.
note:
## Investigation
1. The `message` names the actor and the deleted VM/host.
2. Confirm the deletion was authorised; correlate with the actor's other vCenter activity.
## Response
If unauthorised, restore the VM from backup and investigate the actor for compromise.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"vsphere.log" and message:"Removed" and message:"from NBI-Datacenter" and not message:"Veeam.Backup"

name: VMware vSphere — Virtual Machine Powered Off
description: Detects a virtual machine being powered off in the NBI datacenter. The message names the actor, the VM and the ESXi host. Powering off a production or security VM removes its workload and monitoring — a potential availability-impact or attacker action to disable a defensive system. Routine maintenance is expected; correlate the actor and VM against change control.
note:
## Investigation
1. The `message` names the actor, VM and host. Confirm the shutdown was scheduled/authorised.
2. Prioritise power-offs of production, database or security VMs, and any outside a maintenance window.
## Response
If unauthorised, power the VM back on and investigate the actor account for compromise.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"vsphere.log" and message:"Powered Off" and message:"NBI-Datacenter"

name: Account Creation And Added to Local Group
description: Account Creation And Added to Local Group
query:
sequence  with maxspan=30s
      [any where winlog.event_id == "4720" and user.target.id!= null] by user.target.id
      [any where winlog.task == "Security Group Management" and winlog.event_data.MemberSid !=null] by winlog.event_data.MemberSid

name: Brute Force Attack Detection - IP Threshold
description: Detects potential brute force attacks when an IP address has 100 or more authentication attempts within 5 minutes

name: Brute Force Attacks - Windows
description: Brute Force Attacks - Windows

name: Change Audit — AD Account Lockout (4740)
description: AD - Account Locked

name: Change Audit — Windows Network Share Created, Modified or Deleted
description:
Change objective
Audit creation, modification and deletion of Windows network shares (and share permissions) for change control — new shares can expose data or enable lateral movement.

Detection logic
Windows logs share create/modify/delete with the share name/path and the acting subject. This rule surfaces all share changes as an auditable change feed.

Why this works
Share change events are low-volume and structured, giving a clean change-audit trail for a control that directly affects data exposure.

False positives
Legitimate administrative share management or software installation that creates shares.

Tuning
Correlate each share change with a ticket; escalate new shares on servers hosting sensitive data or unusual share paths.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 5142 (share created), 5143 (share/permissions modified), 5144 (share deleted); winlog.event_data.ShareName, ShareLocalPath, SubjectUserName.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. event.code = create/modify/delete; ShareName/ShareLocalPath = the share; SubjectUserName = actor.
2. Confirm authorization; a new share on a sensitive server, or a permission change opening a share, is higher priority.
false_positives: Legitimate administrative share management or software installation that creates shares.

name: Change Audit — Windows Privileged Group Membership Changed
description:
Change objective
Audit additions to and removals from privileged Windows/AD groups (Administrators, Domain/Enterprise Admins, built-in Operators, Remote Desktop/Management Users, DnsAdmins) for change control.

Detection logic
Membership changes to privileged groups grant or remove significant access. This rule surfaces every add/remove on the privileged group set as an auditable change, complementing the attack-focused Tier-0 addition detection.

Why this works
Group-membership event codes record the group, the member and the actor; scoping to privileged group names/SIDs yields a high-value, low-volume change-audit trail.

False positives
Authorized administration and role rotation.

Tuning
Correlate each change with a change/access-request ticket; additions are higher priority than removals; the attack-focused Tier-0 rule handles the critical additions at high severity.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 4728/4732/4756 (add), 4729/4733/4757 (remove); TargetUserName/TargetSid (group), MemberName/MemberSid (member), SubjectUserName (actor).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. event.code = add/remove; TargetUserName = the privileged group; MemberName = who was added/removed; SubjectUserName = actor.
2. Verify against an access-request/change ticket; correlate additions with the member's subsequent privileged activity.
false_positives: Authorized administration and role rotation.
query: event.code:("4728" or "4729" or "4732" or "4733" or "4756" or "4757") and (winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:(*Admins or *Administrators or *Operators or "Remote Desktop Users" or "Remote Management Users" or DnsAdmins or "Group Policy Creator Owners") or winlog.event_data.TargetSid:("S-1-5-32-544" or "S-1-5-32-548" or "S-1-5-32-549" or "S-1-5-32-550" or "S-1-5-32-551" or "S-1-5-32-552"))

name: Change Audit — Windows System Time Changed by an Interactive Account
description:
Change objective
Audit changes to a host's system clock by an interactive account — time changes can disrupt logging/forensics, Kerberos, and time-sensitive banking processes.

Detection logic
Windows logs system-time changes with the acting subject. Routine changes are made by the time service under machine/SYSTEM context; a change made under an interactive (human) account is a notable, auditable configuration change.

Why this works
Excluding machine/service accounts isolates human-driven time changes, which are rare and worth reviewing.

False positives
A legitimate administrator correcting the clock; a VM time-sync event under an unusual account.

Tuning
Allowlist verified time-administration; correlate with the host's time-sync configuration.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 4616; winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName, PreviousTime, NewTime.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. SubjectUserName = who changed the clock; PreviousTime/NewTime show the shift.
2. A large or unexplained time change under a human account can indicate anti-forensics or misconfiguration — verify.
false_positives: A legitimate administrator correcting the clock; a VM time-sync event under an unusual account.
query: event.code:"4616" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("*$" or "LOCAL SERVICE" or "SYSTEM" or "NETWORK SERVICE")

name: Change Audit — Windows User Account Created/Deleted/Enabled/Disabled/Modified
description:
Change objective
Audit every Windows user-account lifecycle change (create, delete, enable, disable, rename, unlock, modify) for change-control review.

Detection logic
Windows Security logs each account-management action with the acting subject and the target account. This rule surfaces all account lifecycle changes across the estate as an auditable change feed.

Why this works
The account-management event codes are a complete, structured record of user-account changes; scoping to them yields a clean change-audit trail.

False positives
All routine helpdesk/IT account administration — this is an audit feed, expected to be non-zero.

Tuning
Route to a change-audit dashboard rather than paging; correlate each change with a change ticket; escalate creations of privileged or service accounts.

Required telemetry
Windows Security: event.code 4720 (created), 4726 (deleted), 4722 (enabled), 4725 (disabled), 4738 (changed), 4767 (unlocked), 4781 (renamed); winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName (actor), TargetUserName (target).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation / audit guide
1. event.code = the change; SubjectUserName = actor; TargetUserName = the account changed.
2. Confirm the change maps to an authorized ticket; a new/enabled account, especially privileged, is highest priority.
3. Correlate with the actor's logon and the target account's subsequent activity.
false_positives: All routine helpdesk/IT account administration — this is an audit feed, expected to be non-zero.

name: Sysmon Detection Alerts

name: Windows — Account Sign-In Succeeded After Repeated Failures
description: The same source IP failed network sign-in (4625, type 3) for the SAME human account three or more times and then SUCCEEDED (4624, type 3) within 30 minutes — an account whose password was guessed/brute-forced from that origin. Machine accounts (*$) are excluded from THIS specific analytic because NBI telemetry demonstrated the observed fail->success pattern for machine accounts was recurring benign machine-account retry behaviour (e.g. NIM-PY-APV1$), while AD machine-account passwords are automatically managed high-entropy credentials; machine-account credential abuse remains covered by separate account/host-compromise analytics. The auth-aggregator infrastructure is also excluded. This is the compromise companion to the spray primary: it fires regardless of spray breadth, catching a targeted crack even against a single account. Ordered fail->fail->fail->success (EQL sequence) is required so a one-off typo-then-correct does not match.
note:
### Investigation — sign-in succeeded after repeated failures
1. **WHO / TO WHAT** `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` — the account that failed repeatedly then succeeded; `source.ip` the origin; `host.name` the target.
2. **DID WHAT** >=3 failed network sign-ins then a success for the same account+source in 30m = likely a guessed/brute-forced password.
3. **WHY suspicious** a legitimate user rarely fails 3+ times then succeeds; correlate with the spray primary (was this source also spraying other accounts?).
4. **Escalate**: treat the account as potentially compromised — force a password reset, review what the account did after the success (4672/5140/5145, lateral movement). Rule out a known bad-password loop that finally synced (a service/scheduled task with a stale password).
query:
sequence by source.ip, winlog.event_data.TargetUserName with maxspan=30m
  [ any where event.code == "4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName like "*$" and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName != "ANONYMOUS LOGON" and not cidrMatch(source.ip, "10.11.15.0/24", "10.11.101.0/24", "10.11.102.0/24") ]
  [ any where event.code == "4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" ]
  [ any where event.code == "4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" ]
  [ any where event.code == "4624" and winlog.event_data.LogonType == "3" ]

name: Windows — Audit Policy Changed by Interactive Account
description: Detects a change to the Windows system audit policy (4719) made by an interactive/human account rather than a computer account or SYSTEM. Routine audit-policy events come from GPO reapplication under machine/SYSTEM context (0 interactive baseline over 30d). A human changing audit policy typically means an attacker disabling audit subcategories to blind the SOC, or an unauthorised configuration change.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` = the interactive account; `AuditPolicyChanges` shows which subcategory was added/removed (removal = auditing disabled).
2. Any interactive audit-policy change is unexpected — confirm against change control.
## Response
If unauthorised, restore the audit policy (GPO/`auditpol`) and investigate the account for compromise.
author: raadabujaish

technique.name: Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging

query: event.code:"4719" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$ and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"SYSTEM" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"LOCAL SERVICE" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:"NETWORK SERVICE"

name: Browser Process Spawned from an Unusual Parent [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies instances where an unusual process spawns a chrome browser child process. This behavior could be related to malware stealing browser information.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

> **Disclaimer**:
> This investigation guide was created using generative AI technology and has been reviewed to improve its accuracy and relevance. While every effort has been made to ensure its quality, we recommend validating the content and adapting it to suit your specific environment and operational needs.

### Investigating Browser Process Spawned from an Unusual Parent

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the process execution details to confirm that a web browser process (e.g., chrome.exe, msedge.exe, firefox.exe) has an unusual or suspicious parent process. Focus on the process.parent.name, process.name, and process.args fields.
- Examine the command line arguments for signs of remote debugging flags (e.g., --remote-debugging-port, --remote-debugging-pipe) or injected DLLs that could indicate attempts to hijack browser sessions.
- Check whether the parent process is a scripting host (e.g., wscript.exe, cscript.exe), system utility, or unexpected binary (e.g., cmd.exe, rundll32.exe, powershell.exe) rather than the legitimate browser updater or system launcher.
- Investigate if the suspicious parent process has a known reputation or hash linke
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
  process.name : ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe") and
  process.parent.executable != null and process.command_line != null and
  (
  process.command_line :
           ("\"C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft\\Edge\\Application\\msedge.exe\"",
            "\"C:\\Program Files\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\chrome.exe\"",
            "\"C:\\Program Files\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\chrome.exe\" --headless --disable-logging --log-level=3 --v=0",
            "\"C:\\Program Files\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\chrome.exe\" --headless --log-level=3",
            "\"C:\\Program Files\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\chrome.exe\" --headless",
            "\"C:\\Program Files\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\chrome.exe\" --remote-debugging-port=922? --profile-directory=\"Default\"*",
            "\"C:\\Program Files\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\chrome.exe\" --headless --restore-last-session --remote-debugging-port=45452*") or

  (process.args : "--remote-debugging-port=922?" and process.args : "--window-position=-*,-*")
   ) and
  not process.parent.executable :
                         ("C:\\Windows\\explorer.exe",
                          "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\*.exe",
                          "C:\\Program Files\\*.exe",
                          "C:\\Windows\\System32\\rdpinit.exe",
                          "C:\\Windows\\System32\\sihost.exe",
                          "C:\\Windows\\System32\\RuntimeBroker.exe",
                          "C:\\Windows\\System32\\SECOCL64.exe")

name: Execution via Microsoft DotNet ClickOnce Host [NBI-4688]
description: Identifies the execution of DotNet ClickOnce installer via Dfsvc.exe trampoline. Adversaries may take advantage of ClickOnce to proxy execution of malicious payloads via trusted Microsoft processes.
note:
## Coverage

author: raadabujaish
query:

name: Proxy Execution via Console Window Host [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies abuse of the Console Window Host (conhost.exe) to execute commands via proxy. This behavior is used as a defense evasion technique to blend-in malicious activity with legitimate Windows software.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

### Investigating Proxy Execution via Console Window Host

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the conhost child processes and the parent process to identify the initial vector.
- Identify the user account that performed the action and whether it should perform this kind of action.
- Investigate other alerts associated with the user/host during the past 48 hours.
- Validate the activity is not related to planned patches, updates, network administrator activity, or legitimate software installations.
- Assess whether this behavior is prevalent in the environment by looking for similar occurrences across hosts.

### False positive analysis

- This is a dual-use tool, meaning its usage is not inherently malicious. Analysts can dismiss the alert if the administrator is aware of the activity, no other suspicious activity was identified.

### Response and Remediation

- Initiate the incident response process based on the outcome of the triage.
- Isolate the involved host to prevent further post-compromise behavior.
- Run a full antimalware scan. This may reveal additional artifacts left in the system, persistence mechanisms, and malware components.
- Investi
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
 process.name : "conhost.exe" and process.args : "--headless" and
  process.command_line : ("*powershell*", "*cmd *", "*cmd.exe *", "*script*", "*mshta*", "*curl *", "*curl.exe *", "*^*^*^*", "*.bat*", "*.cmd*", "*schtasks*", "*@SSL*", "*http*", "* \\\\*", "*.vbs*", "*.js*", "*mhsta*")

name: Windows — Credential Dumping via Reg.exe
description: Fires when reg.exe is run with save or export against the SAM, SECURITY, or SYSTEM registry hives — the technique for dumping the hives that contain local password hashes and LSA secrets for offline credential extraction. Attackers copy these hives to crack credentials away from the endpoint. The rule matches the reg.exe process arguments. Maps to ATT&CK Credential Access T1003.002 (OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager).
note:
### Investigation
1. Read process.command_line to confirm which hives were saved and where the output was written.
2. Identify the actor (user.name) and host, and whether this user/host performs sanctioned backup/imaging.
3. Inspect process.parent.name — a shell/PowerShell/unknown parent is more suspicious than a known backup tool.
4. Correlate for the output file being read/exfiltrated and for other credential-access activity on the host.
5. Escalate on non-backup context, an unusual parent, or SAM+SYSTEM saved together (the crack-ready pair).

### False positives / benign
Backup and migration tooling occasionally exports SYSTEM/SOFTWARE hives. Distinguish real credential theft by the hive set (SAM plus SYSTEM together is the crack-ready combination, rarely needed by backups), the parent process (sanctioned backup agent versus ad-hoc shell), the actor, and where the output goes. Investigate the context rather than allowlisting reg.exe, a legitimate binary the attacker deliberately abuses (LOLBin).

### Notes
Pending Batch-2 repair: bind the endpoint/4688 index (currently empty) so the rule fires; process.command_line ~52% populated (coverage cap). Local execution: the host IS the origin (no source.ip).
query: process.name : "reg.exe" AND process.args : ("save" OR "export") AND process.args : ("SAM" OR "SECURITY" OR "SYSTEM")

name: Windows — Credential Theft: Registry Hive or NTDS.dit Extraction
description:
Attacker objective
Steal the credential stores directly: the SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM registry hives (local secrets) or NTDS.dit (the entire domain credential database).

Attack logic
Attackers copy the registry hives with reg.exe save, or extract NTDS.dit using ntdsutil IFM, esentutl, diskshadow or a shadow copy, to harvest all account hashes offline.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the extraction commands. Matching hive-save and NTDS-extraction patterns isolates this theft, independent of case.

False positives
A backup or migration process that legitimately exports hives or NTDS (rare and should be scheduled/known).

Tuning
Allowlist verified backup/migration tooling and windows; treat interactive extraction as an incident.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688. NTDS.dit extraction is highest-impact on a Domain Controller.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host, user and command line; on a Domain Controller, NTDS.dit extraction means full domain credential compromise.
2. Isolate the host; if NTDS was extracted, plan a domain-wide credential reset including a double KRBTGT rotation.
3. Locate the output file and any exfiltration.
false_positives: A backup or migration process that legitimately exports hives or NTDS (rare and should be scheduled/known).
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*save*" AND cl LIKE "*hklm*" AND (cl LIKE "*sam*" OR cl LIKE "*security*" OR cl LIKE "*system*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*ntdsutil*" AND (cl LIKE "*ifm*" OR cl LIKE "*create full*" OR cl LIKE "*ac i ntds*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*esentutl*" AND cl LIKE "*ntds*")
   OR cl LIKE "*ntds.dit*"
   OR cl LIKE "*diskshadow*"
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Potential File Transfer via Curl for Windows [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies Curl for Windows making an HTTP request. Adversaries could abuse Curl to download files or upload data to a remote URL.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

### Investigating Potential File Transfer via Curl for Windows

This rule identifies the use of Curl for Windows to download files from a remote URL or post data to a remote site.

#### Possible investigation steps

- Investigate the process execution chain (parent process tree) for unknown processes. Examine their executable files for prevalence, whether they are located in expected locations, and if they are signed with valid digital signatures.
- Identify the user account that performed the action and whether it should perform this kind of action.
- Contact the account owner and confirm whether they are aware of this activity.
- Investigate other alerts associated with the user/host during the past 48 hours.
- Assess whether this behavior is prevalent in the environment by looking for similar occurrences across hosts.
- Examine the details of the dropped file, and whether it was executed.
- Check the reputation of the domain or IP address used to host the downloaded file or if the user downloaded the file from an internal system.
- Retrieve the files' SHA-256 hash values using the PowerShell `Get-FileHash` cmdlet and search for the existence and reputatio
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
  process.executable : (
    "?:\\Windows\\System32\\curl.exe",
    "?:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\curl.exe"
  ) and
  process.command_line : "*http*" and
  process.parent.name : (
    "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe",
    "rundll32.exe", "explorer.exe",
    "conhost.exe", "forfiles.exe",
    "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe",
    "mshta.exe", "hh.exe", "mmc.exe"
  ) and 
  not (
    ?user.id == "S-1-5-18" and
    /* Don't apply the user.id exclusion to Sysmon for compatibility */
    not event.dataset : ("windows.sysmon_operational", "windows.sysmon")
  ) and
  /* Exclude System Integrity Processes for Sysmon */
  not ?winlog.event_data.IntegrityLevel == "System"

name: Potential CVE-2025-33053 Exploitation [NBI-4688]

description: Identifies a suspicious Diagnostics Utility for Internet Explorer child process. This may indicate the successful exploitation of the vulnerability CVE-2025-33053.

## Triage and analysis

### Investigating Potential CVE-2025-33053 Exploitation

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the process details to confirm the suspicious child process was indeed started by iediagcmd.exe.
- Check any URL file type creation before the alert and review the source of those files.
- Investigate the process tree and make sure all descendant processes are terminated.
- Examine the network activity associated with the suspicious process to detect any unauthorized data exfiltration or communication with known malicious IP addresses.
- Assess the system for any additional indicators of compromise, such as unexpected changes in system files or registry keys, which might suggest a broader attack.

### False positive analysis

- This behavior is very rare and should be highly suspicious.

### Response and remediation

- Isolate the affected system from the network to prevent further spread of the potential threat and to contain any malicious activity.
- Terminate the suspicious child process identified in the alert.
- Conduct a thorough scan of the affected system using updated antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to identify and remove any
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
  process.parent.executable : "C:\\Program Files\\Internet Explorer\\iediagcmd.exe" and
  process.name : ("route.exe", "netsh.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "dxdiag.exe", "conhost.exe", "makecab.exe") and
  process.executable != null and
  not process.executable : ("C:\\Windows\\System32\\route.exe",
                            "C:\\Windows\\System32\\netsh.exe",
                            "C:\\Windows\\System32\\ipconfig.exe",
                            "C:\\Windows\\System32\\dxdiag.exe",
                            "C:\\Windows\\System32\\conhost.exe",
                            "C:\\Windows\\System32\\makecab.exe")

name: Windows — Defender / EDR / Firewall Tampering
description:
Attacker objective
Disable or blind endpoint defenses — Microsoft Defender, the EDR sensor, or the host firewall — to evade detection before further action.

Attack logic
Attackers disable real-time protection, add exclusions, remove signatures, stop the AV/EDR service, unload minifilter drivers, or turn off the host firewall.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the tamper commands (Set-MpPreference, MpCmdRun, service stop of the defender/EDR services, netsh firewall off, fltmc unload), independent of case.

False positives
An administrator legitimately reconfiguring Defender or the firewall during maintenance.

Tuning
Correlate with change control; allowlist sanctioned management automation identities; investigate unexpected actors.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host/user and the exact tamper command.
2. Verify against change control; unexplained defense-tampering is a strong pre-attack indicator — treat the host as suspect.
3. Check whether protection was re-enabled and hunt for activity in the blind window.
false_positives: An administrator legitimately reconfiguring Defender or the firewall during maintenance.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*set-mppreference*" AND cl LIKE "*disable*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*add-mppreference*" AND cl LIKE "*exclusion*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*set-mppreference*" AND cl LIKE "*exclusion*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*mpcmdrun*" AND cl LIKE "*removedefinitions*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*stop*" AND (cl LIKE "*windefend*" OR cl LIKE "*wdnissvc*" OR cl LIKE "*sense*" OR cl LIKE "*mssense*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*netsh*" AND cl LIKE "*advfirewall*" AND cl LIKE "*state off*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*netsh*" AND cl LIKE "*firewall*" AND cl LIKE "*opmode*" AND cl LIKE "*disable*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*fltmc*" AND cl LIKE "*unload*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — Discovery of Internet Capabilities via Built-in Tools
description: Identifies the use of built-in tools attackers can use to check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems. These results may be used to determine communication capabilities with C2 servers, or to identify routes, redirectors, and proxy servers.
author: raadabujaish
query:
host.os.type:windows and event.category:process and event.type:start and 
process.name.caseless:("ping.exe" or "tracert.exe" or "pathping.exe") and
not process.args:("127.0.0.1" or "0.0.0.0" or "localhost" or "::1")

name: Windows — DPAPI Master Key Backup Retrieved from a New Host
description: Event 4692 records an attempt to back up the DPAPI master key. Offensive tooling — Mimikatz `dpapi::`, SharpDPAPI and DonPAPI — triggers this event while harvesting the domain backup key in order to decrypt every user's stored browser passwords, certificates, RDP credentials and Credential Manager entries offline. JCB has a routine baseline of roughly 40 such events a day across 87 hosts, so a flat rule would be noisy; this rule instead alerts only when a **host that has not done this in 14 days** starts doing it. No existing rule covers this event code.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Determine whether the host is a workstation performing normal credential-roaming or a server with no reason to touch DPAPI keys.
2. Review 4693 (DPAPI recovery) on the same host and account immediately afterwards — retrieval followed by mass recovery indicates credential harvesting rather than routine operation.
3. Correlate with `Windows — LSASS Memory Dump via Known Credential-Theft Tooling` and `Windows — Credential Theft: Registry Hive or NTDS.dit Extraction` for the same host.
4. If the account involved is privileged, treat the domain DPAPI backup key as potentially compromised.
false_positives: A newly built or newly imaged host performing its first credential-roaming operation.
Certificate enrolment or credential-manager migration activity.
Backup software that legitimately exercises DPAPI.
query: event.code:"4692"

name: Windows — Elastic Agent Service Terminated
description: Identifies the Elastic endpoint agent has stopped and is no longer running on the host. Adversaries may attempt to disable security monitoring tools in an attempt to evade detection or prevention capabilities during an intrusion. This may also indicate an issue with the agent itself and should be addressed to ensure defensive measures are back in a stable state.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where
/* net, sc or wmic stopping or deleting Elastic Agent on Windows */
(event.type == "start" and
  process.name : ("net.exe", "sc.exe", "wmic.exe","powershell.exe","taskkill.exe","PsKill.exe","ProcessHacker.exe") and
  process.args : ("stopservice","uninstall", "stop", "disabled","Stop-Process","terminate","suspend") and
  process.args : ("elasticendpoint", "Elastic Agent","elastic-agent","elastic-endpoint"))
or
/* service or systemctl used to stop Elastic Agent on Linux */
(event.type == "end" and
  (process.name : ("systemctl", "service") and
    process.args : "elastic-agent" and
    process.args : "stop")
  or
  /* pkill , killall used to stop Elastic Agent on Linux */
  ( event.type == "end" and process.name : ("pkill", "killall") and process.args: "elastic-agent")
  or
  /* Unload Elastic Agent extension on MacOS */
  (process.name : "kextunload" and
    process.args : "com.apple.iokit.EndpointSecurity" and
    event.action : "end"))

name: Windows — Event Log Cleared (All Channels)
description:
Detects clearing of a Windows event log — event 1102 for the Security log and event 104 for any other channel. Log clearing is a defence-evasion and anti-forensics action that almost always follows hands-on-keyboard activity.

**This rule exists to correct a coverage gap.** The existing custom rule 'AD/Windows — Security Event Log Cleared' searches for event 1102 in `logs-system.security-*`, but at JCB the Elastic Windows integration routes 1102 and 104 into the `system.application` and `system.system` datasets, not `system.security`. That rule therefore cannot fire. This rule searches all three system datasets, which is where the events actually land (validated: 16 x 1102 and 971 x 104 over 90 days).
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `winlog.channel` identifies which log was cleared; `winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName` (1102) identifies who cleared it.
2. Reconstruct what the account did **before** the clear using every other telemetry source — the local log is by definition gone. Use FortiGate traffic, share access on other hosts, and the account's activity on the domain controllers.
3. Log clearing on the Exchange servers at JCB has a small routine baseline; log clearing anywhere else, or by an interactive user account, should be escalated.
4. Correlate with `Windows — Defender / EDR / Firewall Tampering` and `Windows — Elastic Agent Service Terminated` on the same host.

### Follow-up
Retire or fix the older 'AD/Windows — Security Event Log Cleared' rule so the SOC is not relying on a query that cannot match.
false_positives: Scheduled log maintenance or log rotation. The Entra/AD Connect server hq-adsync-app-p clears its Application log routinely (68 events in 7 days) and is excluded in the query; Exchange has a small 1102 baseline that is deliberately NOT excluded.
Server rebuilds and imaging.
Diagnostic work by administrators who clear a noisy log before reproducing a fault.
query: event.code:("1102" or "104") and not (event.code:"104" and host.name:"hq-adsync-app-p" and winlog.channel:"Application")

name: Excessive User Account Lockouts
description: Detects excessive user account lockouts (brute force indicator)
query:
FROM logs-* | WHERE event.code == "4740" 
| WHERE user.name NOT LIKE "*$" AND user.name NOT LIKE "svc_*"
| STATS lockout_count = count() BY user.name, host.name 
| WHERE lockout_count > 10

name: Windows — Executable or Script Written to an Administrative Share (Lateral Tool Transfer)
description: Detects a remote write of an executable, library or script onto the C$ or ADMIN$ administrative share. This is the staging half of lateral movement (ATT&CK T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer) and immediately precedes remote service or scheduled-task execution. Built on Windows Security event 5145 with the WriteData access mask, so it requires neither Sysmon nor Elastic Defend. Over the validation window the only accounts performing this were the Nessus scanner and ManageEngine, both excluded, leaving a clean zero baseline.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `winlog.event_data.RelativeTargetName` is the file dropped, relative to the share root; `host.name` is the **destination**.
2. Recover the source IP by joining `winlog.event_data.SubjectLogonId` to event 4624 on the same host.
3. Check for execution of the dropped file: 4688/Sysmon 1 on the destination, or a new service (7045/4697) referencing it.
4. A `.exe` or `.dll` written into `System32`, `SysWOW64` or `Windows\Temp` by an interactive user account is high-confidence malicious.

### Tuning
Exclude specific deployment service accounts by name; do not remove the extension filter.
false_positives: Authenticated vulnerability scanning and agent deployment (Nessus, ManageEngine) — excluded by account.
Software distribution platforms pushing binaries over admin shares.
Backup or patch tooling staging files remotely.
query: event.code:"5145" and winlog.event_data.ShareName:(*C$ or *ADMIN$) and winlog.event_data.AccessList:*WriteData* and winlog.event_data.RelativeTargetName:(*.exe or *.dll or *.bat or *.cmd or *.ps1 or *.vbs or *.js or *.scr or *.msi or *.jar or *.hta) and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("Nessus" or "manageengine" or "svc_nessus" or "scanuser") and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$

name: Windows — Execution of an Unsigned Service
description: This rule identifies the execution of unsigned executables via service control manager (SCM). Adversaries may abuse SCM to execute malware or escalate privileges.
author: raadabujaish
query:
