name: Windows — Ingress Tool Transfer via LOLBin
description:
Attacker objective
Download attacker tooling or a second-stage payload onto a compromised host using a trusted built-in binary (living off the land).

Attack logic
Rather than a browser, attackers fetch files with certutil, bitsadmin, mshta, curl/wget, or PowerShell download methods so the transfer blends in with system activity.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the LOLBin and its URL/output arguments; matching download-specific argument patterns isolates ingress transfers, independent of case.

False positives
An administrator or software-management process legitimately downloading with these tools.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned software-distribution hosts/accounts; review the destination URL for reputation.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Review the URL, the destination path and the requesting host/user.
2. If the source is untrusted, retrieve the downloaded file, isolate the host and hunt for execution of the payload.
false_positives: An administrator or software-management process legitimately downloading with these tools.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*certutil*" AND (cl LIKE "*urlcache*" OR cl LIKE "*verifyctl*" OR cl LIKE "*-split*") AND cl LIKE "*http*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*bitsadmin*" AND (cl LIKE "*transfer*" OR cl LIKE "*addfile*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*mshta*" AND cl LIKE "*http*")
   OR ((cl LIKE "*curl *" OR cl LIKE "*wget *") AND cl LIKE "*http*" AND (cl LIKE "*-o*" OR cl LIKE "*-outfile*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*powershell*" AND (cl LIKE "*downloadfile*" OR cl LIKE "*downloadstring*" OR cl LIKE "*invoke-webrequest*" OR cl LIKE "*start-bitstransfer*") AND cl LIKE "*http*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — Inhibit System Recovery (Ransomware Precursor)
description:
Attacker objective
Destroy backups and recovery options (shadow copies, boot recovery, backup catalog) so victims cannot restore — the hallmark preparation step of ransomware.

Attack logic
Before or during encryption, ransomware deletes Volume Shadow Copies, disables Windows boot recovery, and removes backup catalogs to maximize damage and prevent restoration.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records these destructive commands (vssadmin/wmic shadow delete, bcdedit recovery-off, wbadmin delete), independent of case.

False positives
A backup administrator legitimately pruning shadow storage or catalogs (should be scheduled/known).

Tuning
Allowlist verified backup automation and windows; treat interactive or unexpected execution as an active ransomware incident.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Treat as a likely in-progress ransomware event: isolate the host immediately.
2. Identify the user/parent process and any mass file modification; preserve evidence and invoke IR.
3. Check other hosts for the same command pattern (worming/estate-wide deployment).
false_positives: A backup administrator legitimately pruning shadow storage or catalogs (should be scheduled/known).
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*vssadmin*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*" AND cl LIKE "*shadow*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*vssadmin*" AND cl LIKE "*resize*" AND cl LIKE "*shadowstorage*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*wmic*" AND cl LIKE "*shadowcopy*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*win32_shadowcopy*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*bcdedit*" AND (cl LIKE "*recoveryenabled*no*" OR cl LIKE "*bootstatuspolicy*ignoreallfailures*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*wbadmin*" AND cl LIKE "*delete*" AND (cl LIKE "*catalog*" OR cl LIKE "*systemstatebackup*" OR cl LIKE "*backup*"))
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — LSASS Memory Dump via Known Credential-Theft Tooling
description:
Attacker objective
Dump the memory of the LSASS process to extract plaintext credentials, hashes and Kerberos tickets.

Attack logic
LSASS holds credential material for logged-on users. Attackers dump its memory with tools such as procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, nanodump, or built-in minidump routines, then extract secrets offline.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the tool and its arguments. Matching known LSASS-dump tool/argument patterns targeting lsass isolates credential theft, independent of case.

False positives
Legitimate crash-diagnostic tooling explicitly dumping lsass (rare). A renamed dumping tool would still match on the lsass/MiniDump argument pattern.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned diagnostic hosts/accounts; treat any hands-on-keyboard lsass dump as an incident.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688 (process.command_line).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host, user and full command line; confirm the target is lsass.
2. Treat the host as compromised: isolate, rotate credentials of all accounts logged on to that host, and begin IR.
3. Hunt for the dumped file and any exfiltration or offline-cracking follow-on.
false_positives: Legitimate crash-diagnostic tooling explicitly dumping lsass (rare). A renamed dumping tool would still match on the lsass/MiniDump argument pattern.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*lsass*" AND (cl LIKE "*procdump*" OR cl LIKE "*minidump*" OR cl LIKE "*nanodump*" OR cl LIKE "*dumpert*" OR cl LIKE "*sqldumper*" OR cl LIKE "*createdump*" OR cl LIKE "*rdrleakdiag*" OR cl LIKE "*avdump*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*comsvcs*" AND (cl LIKE "*minidump*" OR cl LIKE "*#24*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*rundll32*" AND cl LIKE "*comsvcs*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — Malicious PowerShell: AMSI/ETW Bypass or Offensive Tooling
description:
Attacker objective
Run offensive PowerShell in memory — bypassing AMSI/ETW inspection, dumping credentials, roasting Kerberos, or enumerating the domain.

Attack logic
Attacker frameworks disable AMSI/ETW and load credential-theft, Kerberos-abuse, enumeration and injection modules. Script-block logging records the expanded script even when it was launched obfuscated or base64-encoded.

Why this detection works
PowerShell 4104 captures the decoded script-block text, so matching known offensive markers detects the activity despite encoding or obfuscation.

False positives
Security testing, or a defensive script that references these strings by name. Bare Net.WebClient/download usage is excluded as too common.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned red-team/testing windows; treat production hits as incidents.

Required telemetry
PowerShell Operational 4104 (script-block logging must be enabled).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Read the full script-block text to confirm intent (AMSI bypass, credential theft, enumeration).
2. Identify the host/user; if malicious, isolate and rotate credentials used on that host.
3. Correlate with process-creation, logon and outbound-network telemetry for the same host/time.
false_positives: Security testing, or a defensive script that references these strings by name. Bare Net.WebClient/download usage is excluded as too common.
query: event.code:"4104" and powershell.file.script_block_text:("amsiInitFailed" or "AmsiUtils" or "amsiContext" or "AmsiScanBuffer" or "EtwEventWrite" or "sekurlsa" or "logonpasswords" or "Invoke-Mimikatz" or "Invoke-Kerberoast" or "Rubeus" or "Invoke-BloodHound" or "SharpHound" or "Get-DomainUser" or "Get-NetComputer" or "PowerView" or "Invoke-ReflectivePEInjection" or "Invoke-DllInjection" or "Out-Minidump" or "Invoke-TokenManipulation")

process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
 process.name : ("rundll32.exe", "mshta.exe") and
  (
     (process.command_line :
        (
        "*script*eval(*",
         "*script*GetObject*",
         "*.regread(*",
         "*WScript.Shell*",
         "*.run(*",
         "*).Exec()*",
         "*mshta*http*",
         "*mshtml*RunHTMLApplication*",
         "*mshtml*,#135*",
         "*StrReverse*",
         "*.RegWrite*",
         /* Issue #379 */
         "*window.close(*",
         "* Chr(*"
         )
     and not ?process.parent.executable :
                  ("?:\\Program Files (x86)\\Citrix\\System32\\wfshell.exe",
                   "?:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft Office\\Office*\\MSACCESS.EXE",
                   "?:\\Program Files\\Quokka.Works GTInstaller\\GTInstaller.exe")
     ) or

    (process.name : "mshta.exe" and
     not process.command_line : ("*.hta*", "*.htm*", "-Embedding") and ?process.args_count >=2) or

     /* Execution of HTA file downloaded from the internet */
     (process.name : "mshta.exe" and process.command_line : "*\\Users\\*\\Downloads\\*.hta*") or

     /* Execution of HTA file from archive */
     (process.name : "mshta.exe" and
      process.args : ("?:\\Users\\*\\Temp\\7z*", "?:\\Users\\*\\Temp\\Rar$*", "?:\\Users\\*\\Temp\\Temp?_*", "?:\\Users\\*\\Temp\\BNZ.*"))
   )

name: Windows — Netsh Helper DLL
description: Identifies the addition of a Netsh Helper DLL, netsh.exe supports the addition of these DLLs to extend its functionality. Attackers may abuse this mechanism to execute malicious payloads every time the utility is executed, which can be done by administrators or a scheduled task.
author: raadabujaish
query:
registry where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "change" and
  registry.path : (
    "HKLM\\Software\\Microsoft\\netsh\\*",
    "\\REGISTRY\\MACHINE\\Software\\Microsoft\\netsh\\*"
  )

name: Windows — Network-Level Authentication (NLA) Disabled
description: Identifies the attempt to disable Network-Level Authentication (NLA) via registry modification. Network Level Authentication (NLA) is a feature on Windows that provides an extra layer of security for Remote Desktop (RDP) connections, as it requires users to authenticate before allowing a full RDP session. Attackers can disable NLA to enable persistence methods that require access to the Windows sign-in screen without authenticating, such as Accessibility Features persistence methods, like Sticky Keys.
author: raadabujaish
query:
registry where host.os.type == "windows" and event.action != "deletion" and
  registry.path :
       ("HKLM\\SYSTEM\\ControlSet*\\Control\\Terminal Server\\WinStations\\RDP-Tcp\\UserAuthentication", 
        "\\REGISTRY\\MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\*ControlSet*\\Control\\Terminal Server\\WinStations\\RDP-Tcp\\UserAuthentication" ) and
  registry.data.strings : "0"

name: Initial Access — New RDP User→Host Pair (Remote Interactive Logon)
description: First-ever RDP (Type 10) logon of a given user to a given host in the last 14 days. Low severity on its own (seed activity through a shared gateway is common) but correlates with later spray/Kerberoast/lateral movement in the multi-stage rule to elevate.
note:
### Investigation
1. Expected for this user to RDP this host?
2. Correlate source.ip and subsequent privileged/lateral activity (multi-stage rule).
### Tuning
Suppression via new_terms 14d window; a busy admin will only alert on genuinely new destinations.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Users legitimately accessing a new server for the first time (expected background rate; low severity by design).
query: event.code:"4624" and winlog.event_data.LogonType:"10" and source.ip:* and not source.ip:"::1"

name: Non-Admin Edited a Security-enabled Group
description: Detects non-admin users modifying security groups
query: (event.code : "4728" OR event.code : "4729" OR event.code : "4730") AND NOT (user.name : *admin* OR *ADMIN*)

name: Windows — Offensive / Dual-Use Tooling Executed (Process Name — Covers Hosts Without Command-Line Auditing)
description: Detects execution of well-known credential-theft, discovery, tunnelling, remote-access and anti-forensics tooling by **process name only**. This deliberately avoids `process.command_line`, which at JCB is populated on just 119 of the 288 hosts that emit event 4688 (19% of events) because the 'Include command line in process creation events' policy is not applied fleet-wide. Every existing command-line-based rule is blind on the remaining 169 hosts; this rule restores baseline coverage there. Validated baseline over 14 days: 3 events (csvde.exe on a domain controller, netscan.exe and procdump.exe on workstations) — all of which are themselves worth investigating.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `process.name` names the tool; `process.parent.name` shows how it was launched (a browser, Office, or a shell parent raises severity).
2. `winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName` is the invoking account — confirm it belongs to a person authorised to run security tooling.
3. Remote-access tools (AnyDesk, RustDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera) on a banking endpoint are a common initial-access and ransomware-affiliate pattern — verify against the approved software list.
4. Tunnelling tools (ngrok, frp, chisel, plink, gost) indicate command-and-control or data-egress preparation; pivot to FortiGate traffic for the same host.

### Tuning
If the bank's IT or security team legitimately runs a tool from this list, remove that single value or add a host/user exception — do not disable the rule. Renamed binaries will evade it, which is precisely why fleet-wide command-line auditing is also recommended.
false_positives: Authorised penetration testing or internal red-team activity.
IT administrators using Sysinternals, nmap or Advanced IP Scanner for legitimate diagnostics.
Approved remote-support software, if any of the listed products are sanctioned at JCB.
query: event.code:("4688" or "1") and process.name:(mimikatz.exe or mimilib.dll or procdump.exe or procdump64.exe or rubeus.exe or sharphound.exe or bloodhound.exe or psexec.exe or psexec64.exe or psexesvc.exe or paexec.exe or remcom.exe or csexec.exe or winexesvc.exe or secretsdump.exe or wce.exe or fgdump.exe or pwdump.exe or gsecdump.exe or lazagne.exe or nanodump.exe or dumpert.exe or seatbelt.exe or winpeas.exe or winpeas64.exe or sharpup.exe or powerup.exe or sharpview.exe or sharphound3.exe or juicypotato.exe or printspoofer.exe or rottenpotato.exe or godpotato.exe or sweetpotato.exe or certipy.exe or certify.exe or kerbrute.exe or crackmapexec.exe or nltestk.exe or adfind.exe or advanced_port_scanner.exe or advanced_ip_scanner.exe or netscan.exe or softperfect.exe or nmap.exe or masscan.exe or nc.exe or ncat.exe or netcat.exe or plink.exe or ngrok.exe or frp.exe or frpc.exe or frps.exe or chisel.exe or gost.exe or htran.exe or rclone.exe or megasync.exe or anydesk.exe or rustdesk.exe or atera.exe or screenconnect.exe or meshagent.exe or sdelete.exe or sdelete64.exe or rdpwrap.exe)

name: Windows — Office Application Spawned a Command Shell or Script Host
description: Detects a Microsoft Office application spawning a command shell or scripting host (cmd, PowerShell, wscript/cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32). This parent-child relationship is a hallmark of malicious-macro / phishing-document execution.
note:
## Investigation
1. `process.parent.name` (Office app) spawned `process.name`.
2. Review `process.command_line` for the downloaded/executed payload.
3. Correlate with the source document and the user's recent email; check for follow-on network or PowerShell activity.
## Response
Isolate the host, capture the document, and reset the user's credentials if execution succeeded.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"4688" and process.parent.name:("winword.exe" or "excel.exe" or "powerpnt.exe" or "outlook.exe" or "onenote.exe" or "msaccess.exe") and process.name:("cmd.exe" or "powershell.exe" or "pwsh.exe" or "wscript.exe" or "cscript.exe" or "mshta.exe" or "rundll32.exe" or "regsvr32.exe" or "bitsadmin.exe" or "certutil.exe")

name: Windows — Office Test Registry Persistence
description: Identifies the modification of the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key, a registry location that can be used to specify a DLL which will be executed every time an MS Office application is started. Attackers can abuse this to gain persistence on a compromised host.
author: raadabujaish
query:
registry where host.os.type == "windows" and event.action != "deletion" and
    registry.path : "*\\Software\\Microsoft\\Office Test\\Special\\Perf\\*"

name: Proxy Execution via Windows OpenSSH [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies attempts to execute commands via proxy using the Windows OpenSSH client. This may indicate an attempt to bypass application control via trusted windows binaries.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

### Investigating Proxy Execution via Windows OpenSSH

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the ssh child processes and the parent process to identify the initial vector.
- Identify the user account that performed the action and whether it should perform this kind of action.
- Investigate other alerts associated with the user/host during the past 48 hours.
- Validate the activity is not related to planned patches, updates, network administrator activity, or legitimate software installations.
- Assess whether this behavior is prevalent in the environment by looking for similar occurrences across hosts.

### False positive analysis

- This is a dual-use tool, meaning its usage is not inherently malicious. Analysts can dismiss the alert if the administrator is aware of the activity, no other suspicious activity was identified.

### Response and Remediation

- Initiate the incident response process based on the outcome of the triage.
- Isolate the involved host to prevent further post-compromise behavior.
- Run a full antimalware scan. This may reveal additional artifacts left in the system, persistence mechanisms, and malware components.
- Investigate cre
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and process.name : ("ssh.exe", "sftp.exe") and
 process.command_line : ("*Command=*powershell*", "*schtasks*", "*Command=*@echo off*", "*Command=*http*", "*Command=*mshta*",  "*Command=*msiexec*",
                          "*Command=*cmd /c*", "*Command=*cmd.exe*", "*Command=\"cmd /c*", "*LocalCommand=scp*&&*", "*LocalCommand=?scp*&&*", "*Command=*script*")

name: Windows — Password Spray From a Single Source
description: One source IP failed network sign-in (Windows 4625, logon type 3) against 10 or more DISTINCT accounts within an hour — the fan-out signature of password spraying. NBI's normal auth-failure baseline is dominated by stuck credentials (one source, one-two accounts) and by auth-aggregator infrastructure (the scanwave vulnerability scanner, VDI/RDS farms on 10.11.101.0/24 and 10.11.102.0/24, and app/Citrix servers on 10.11.15.0/24) which legitimately touch many accounts; those are excluded as an evidence-backed category (known_infrastructure:auth-aggregators). Keyed on DISTINCT-account cardinality per source (not raw failure volume), so a stuck-credential loop that fails one account thousands of times does NOT match, while a spray across many accounts does. source.ip is ~71% populated on 4625 (network logons carry it); local failures without a source are out of scope for this analytic.
note:
### Investigation — password spray from one source
1. **WHO / FROM WHERE** `source.ip` — is it a workstation/server that has no business attempting sign-in to many accounts? Resolve the host; a normal endpoint fails 1–2 accounts, not 10+.
2. **DID WHAT / TO WHAT** the rule fired because this source failed >=10 DISTINCT accounts in an hour. Pull the target accounts (4625 `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` for this source) — are they enumerated/sequential or a real user population?
3. **WHY suspicious** breadth: one origin touching many identities = spray. Check `winlog.event_data.SubStatus` (0xc000006a bad-password across many users = spray; 0xc0000064 user-not-exist = enumeration).
4. **Escalate** if any of the sprayed accounts then SUCCEEDS (4624) from this source — that is a compromise (see the brute-force-success companion). De-escalate only after confirming the source is a newly-added, sanctioned auth aggregator; then add it to known_infrastructure by evidence, not as a blanket allowlist.
query: event.code:"4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType:"3" and source.ip:* and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:"ANONYMOUS LOGON" and not source.ip:"10.11.15.0/24" and not source.ip:"10.11.101.0/24" and not source.ip:"10.11.102.0/24"

name: Windows — Potential LSA Authentication Package Abuse
description: Adversaries can use the autostart mechanism provided by the Local Security Authority (LSA) authentication packages for privilege escalation or persistence by placing a reference to a binary in the Windows registry. The binary will then be executed by SYSTEM when the authentication packages are loaded.
author: raadabujaish
query:
registry where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "change" and
  registry.path : (
      "HKLM\\SYSTEM\\*ControlSet*\\Control\\Lsa\\Authentication Packages",
      "\\REGISTRY\\MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\*ControlSet*\\Control\\Lsa\\Authentication Packages"
  ) and
  /* exclude SYSTEM SID - look for changes by non-SYSTEM user */
  not user.id : "S-1-5-18"

name: Windows — Potential Ransomware Behavior - High count of Readme files by System
description: This rule identifies a high number (20) of file creation event by the System virtual process from the same host and with same file name containing keywords similar to ransomware note files and all within a short time period.
author: raadabujaish
query:
event.category:file and host.os.type:windows and process.pid:4 and event.action:creation and
 file.name:(*read*me* or *README* or *lock* or *LOCK* or *how*to* or *HOW*TO* or *@* or *recover* or *RECOVER* or *decrypt* or *DECRYPT* or *restore* or *RESTORE* or *FILES_BACK* or *files_back*)

name: Windows — Potential SharpRDP Behavior
description: Identifies potential behavior of SharpRDP, which is a tool that can be used to perform authenticated command execution against a remote target via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) for the purposes of lateral movement.
author: raadabujaish
query:
/* Incoming RDP followed by a new RunMRU string value set to cmd, powershell, taskmgr or tsclient, followed by process execution within 1m */

sequence by host.id with maxspan=1m
  [network where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and process.name : "svchost.exe" and destination.port == 3389 and
   network.direction : ("incoming", "ingress") and network.transport == "tcp" and
   source.ip != "127.0.0.1" and source.ip != "::1"
  ]

  [registry where host.os.type == "windows" and process.name : "explorer.exe" and
   registry.path : ("HKEY_USERS\\*\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Explorer\\RunMRU\\*") and
   registry.data.strings : ("cmd.exe*", "powershell.exe*", "taskmgr*", "\\\\tsclient\\*.exe\\*")
  ]

  [process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
   (process.parent.name : ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "taskmgr.exe") or process.args : ("\\\\tsclient\\*.exe")) and
   not process.name : "conhost.exe"
   ]

name: Powershell DownloadFile
description: Detects PowerShell DownloadFile activity
query: process.name : "powershell.exe" AND process.args : "*DownloadFile*"

name: Malicious PowerShell Process - Encoded Command
description: Detects PowerShell with encoded commands
query: process.name : "powershell.exe" AND process.args : ("-EncodedCommand" OR "-enc")

name: Malicious PowerShell Process - Execution Policy Bypass
description: Detects PowerShell execution policy bypass attempts
query: process.name : "powershell.exe" AND process.args : ("-ExecutionPolicy" OR "-ep" OR "Bypass")

name: Remote Desktop File Opened from Suspicious Path [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies attempts to open a remote desktop file from suspicious paths. Adversaries may abuse RDP files for initial access.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

> **Disclaimer**:
> This investigation guide was created using generative AI technology and has been reviewed to improve its accuracy and relevance. While every effort has been made to ensure its quality, we recommend validating the content and adapting it to suit your specific environment and operational needs.

### Investigating Remote Desktop File Opened from Suspicious Path

Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) allows users to connect to and control a computer remotely, facilitating remote work and administration. However, adversaries can exploit RDP files, which store connection settings, to gain unauthorized access. They may distribute malicious RDP files via phishing, placing them in suspicious directories. The detection rule identifies when RDP files are opened from unusual paths, signaling potential misuse and enabling analysts to investigate further.

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the process execution details to confirm the presence of "mstsc.exe" and verify the suspicious path from which the RDP file was opened, as specified in the query.
- Check the user account associated with the process to determine if the activity aligns with their typ
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
 process.name : "mstsc.exe" and
 process.args : ("?:\\Users\\*\\Downloads\\*.rdp",
                 "?:\\Users\\*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\Temp?_*.rdp",
                 "?:\\Users\\*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\7z*.rdp",
                 "?:\\Users\\*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\Rar$*\\*.rdp",
                 "?:\\Users\\*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\BNZ.*.rdp",
                 "?:\\Users\\*\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\Windows\\INetCache\\Content.Outlook\\*.rdp")

name: Cmdline Tool Not Executed In CMD Shell
description: Detects suspicious execution of command-line tools outside cmd.exe
query: process.parent.name : "powershell.exe" AND process.name : ("whoami" OR "ipconfig" OR "tasklist" OR "systeminfo")

name: Windows — Registry Persistence: IFEO / Winlogon / AppInit
description:
Attacker objective
Persist or hijack execution by writing a boot/logon or image-hijack registry value — Image File Execution Options debugger, Winlogon Shell/Userinit, or AppInit_DLLs.

Attack logic
Setting an IFEO Debugger launches attacker code whenever a target program runs; changing Winlogon Shell/Userinit or AppInit_DLLs loads attacker code at logon or into processes. These keys are rarely modified legitimately.

Why this detection works
Registry-modification auditing records the key path and value name; scoping to the specific persistence values isolates the technique.

False positives
A debugging tool that legitimately sets an IFEO Debugger, or a management agent modifying Userinit (rare).

Tuning
Allowlist verified management tooling; investigate any unexpected write to these values.

Required telemetry
Sysmon Event ID 13 (registry.path, registry.value). Covers hosts running Sysmon.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Identify the host and the value written (Debugger / Shell / Userinit / AppInit_DLLs) and its data.
2. If the data points to an attacker binary/script, remove it and investigate the writing process and user.
false_positives: A debugging tool that legitimately sets an IFEO Debugger, or a management agent modifying Userinit (rare).
query: event.code:"13" and ((registry.path:"*Image File Execution Options*" and registry.value:("Debugger" or "GlobalFlag")) or registry.value:"AppInit_DLLs" or (registry.path:"*Winlogon*" and registry.value:("Shell" or "Userinit" or "Notify")))

name: Query Registry using Built-in Tools [NBI-4688]
description: This rule identifies the execution of commands that can be used to query the Windows Registry. Adversaries may query the registry to gain situational awareness about the host, like installed security software, programs and settings.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.
author: raadabujaish
query:
host.os.type:windows and event.category:process and event.type:start and
  (
    (process.name.caseless:"reg.exe" and process.args:"query") or
    (process.name.caseless:("powershell.exe" or "powershell_ise.exe" or "pwsh.exe") and
     process.args:(
       ("get-childitem" or "Get-ChildItem" or "gci" or "dir" or "ls" or
        "get-item" or "Get-Item" or "gi" or
        "get-itemproperty" or "Get-ItemProperty" or "gp") and
       ("hkcu" or "HKCU" or "hkey_current_user" or "HKEY_CURRENT_USER" or
        "hkey_local_machine" or "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE" or
        "hklm" or "HKLM" or registry\:\:*)
      )
    )
  ) and
  not process.command_line : (
    "C:\\Windows\\system32\\reg.exe  query hklm\\software\\microsoft\\windows\\softwareinventorylogging /v collectionstate /reg:64" or
    "reg  query \"HKLM\\Software\\WOW6432Node\\Npcap\" /ve  "
  )

name: Windows — Remote-Execution Service Installed on a New Host (PsExec / PAExec / RemCom Family)
description:
Detects installation of a service whose name matches the remote-execution tool families used for lateral movement: Sysinternals PsExec (PSEXESVC), PAExec, RemCom, CSExec, winexe and Impacket. Uses System-channel event 7045, which records ServiceName, ImagePath and the account the service runs as. This complements the existing 4697-based image-path rule by keying on the tool's service name instead, and covers hosts where Security-channel service auditing is not enabled.

**Why new_terms rather than a plain query:** the authenticated Nessus scanner installs PSEXESVC across the estate as part of its credentialed checks — 110 events on 51 hosts in 7 days. Event 7045 carries no actor field, so the scanner cannot be excluded by account name the way it can on event 5145. Keying on a previously unseen host/service pair over a 14-day history suppresses the recurring scan targets while still alerting the first time PsExec lands on a host that has not seen it before.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. `winlog.event_data.ImagePath` shows the binary; `winlog.event_data.AccountName` shows the run-as context (usually LocalSystem).
2. Identify who created it: correlate with 4697 and with 5145 `svcctl`/`PSEXESVC` access on the same host and timeframe.
3. PsExec-family services are normally installed and removed within seconds — look for a matching 7036/7045 delete.
4. Establish whether the bank's IT team uses PsExec for support; if not, treat as hands-on-keyboard intrusion.
false_positives: IT administrators using Sysinternals PsExec for legitimate remote administration.
Authenticated vulnerability scanning that installs a temporary service.
Remote support tooling built on the PsExec service model.
query: event.code:"7045" and winlog.event_data.ServiceName:("PSEXESVC" or "PAExec*" or "RemCom*" or "CSExec*" or "BTOBTO" or "winexesvc" or "PsExec*" or "impacket*" or "SecretsDump*")

name: Windows — Remote Execution via WMI or WinRM
description:
Attacker objective
Execute commands on a remote host over WMI or WinRM/PowerShell-Remoting to move laterally after a foothold.

Attack logic
Remote WMI process creation runs children under WmiPrvSE; WinRM/PS-Remoting runs them under wsmprovhost/winrshost. A shell, scripting host or recon/download tool spawned by these service hosts indicates remote command execution.

Why this detection works
Process-creation lineage ties the WMI/WinRM host process to a suspicious child on the same event, isolating remote execution from local activity.

False positives
Legitimate remote administration and management tooling that uses WMI/WinRM.

Tuning
Allowlist sanctioned management/monitoring source hosts and service accounts; a burst across many destination hosts is higher-risk.

Required telemetry
Process creation with parent process: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. The parent (WmiPrvSE/wsmprovhost) launched a shell/tool — remote WMI/WinRM execution.
2. Identify the initiating host/user (correlate with 4624 network logons and 5145 shares) and the child command.
3. If unauthorised, treat as lateral movement and isolate both source and destination.
false_positives: Legitimate remote administration and management tooling that uses WMI/WinRM.
query: process where event.code in ("1","4688") and process.parent.name in~ ("wmiprvse.exe","wsmprovhost.exe","winrshost.exe") and process.name in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","nltest.exe","schtasks.exe","sc.exe")

name: Windows — Remote File Download via PowerShell
description: Identifies powershell.exe being used to download an executable file from an untrusted remote destination.
author: raadabujaish
query:
sequence by process.entity_id with maxspan=30s

[network where host.os.type == "windows" and
  process.name : ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "powershell_ise.exe") and network.protocol == "dns" and
   not dns.question.name : (
          "localhost", "*.microsoft.com", "*.azureedge.net", "*.powershellgallery.com",
          "*.windowsupdate.com", "metadata.google.internal", "dist.nuget.org",
          "artifacts.elastic.co", "*.digicert.com", "packages.chocolatey.org",
          "outlook.office365.com"
       ) and not user.id : "S-1-5-18"]
[file where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "creation" and
  process.name : "powershell.exe" and file.extension : ("exe", "dll", "ps1", "bat") and
  not file.name : "__PSScriptPolicy*.ps1"]

name: Potential Remote Install via MsiExec [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies attempts to install a file from a remote server using MsiExec. Adversaries may abuse Windows Installers for initial access and delivery of malware.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

> **Disclaimer**:
> This investigation guide was created using generative AI technology and has been reviewed to improve its accuracy and relevance. While every effort has been made to ensure its quality, we recommend validating the content and adapting it to suit your specific environment and operational needs.

### Investigating Potential Remote Install via MsiExec

MsiExec is a Windows utility for installing, maintaining, and removing software. Adversaries exploit it to execute malicious payloads by disguising them as legitimate installations. The detection rule identifies suspicious child processes spawned by MsiExec that initiate network activity, which is atypical for standard installations. By focusing on unusual executable paths and network connections, the rule helps uncover potential misuse indicative of malware delivery or initial access attempts.

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the process tree to identify the parent and child processes of the suspicious MsiExec activity, focusing on the process.entity_id and process.parent.name fields to understand the execution flow.
- Examine the process.executable path to determine if it deviates
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
  process.name : "msiexec.exe" and process.args : ("-i", "/i") and process.command_line : "*http*" and
  process.args : ("/qn", "-qn", "-q", "/q", "/quiet") and
  process.parent.name : ("sihost.exe", "explorer.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "powershell.exe", "wmiprvse.exe", "pcalua.exe", "forfiles.exe", "conhost.exe") and
  not process.command_line : ("*--set-server=*", "*UPGRADEADD=*" , "*--url=*",
                              "*USESERVERCONFIG=*", "*RCTENTERPRISESERVER=*", "*app.ninjarmm.com*", "*zoom.us/client*",
                              "*SUPPORTSERVERSTSURI=*", "*START_URL=*", "*AUTOCONFIG=*", "*awscli.amazonaws.com*")

name: Windows — Remote SAM Enumeration via SMB Named Pipe
description: Detects remote binding to the SAMR named pipe over SMB by an interactive user account. SAMR backs the account and group enumeration performed by BloodHound/SharpHound, net.exe, rpcclient and Impacket samrdump, used to inventory domain users, groups and privileges before privilege escalation. Machine accounts and known scanner accounts are excluded because they generate this traffic routinely at JCB. Validated baseline after exclusions: 3 events across 7 days. The `lsarpc` and `netlogon` pipes were deliberately excluded from this rule — a single monitoring account generates ~230,000 lsarpc binds per week at JCB, which would render the rule unusable.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Confirm whether the account is an administrator performing legitimate directory work.
2. Volume matters: a single bind is routine, dozens of binds across many hosts in minutes indicates automated enumeration.
3. Pivot to `AD — Domain Reconnaissance via LOLBins / BloodHound` and PowerShell 4104 activity for the same user.
4. Check whether the same account subsequently appears in Tier-0 group changes or Kerberoasting alerts.
false_positives: Vulnerability scanners and inventory tools (excluded by account name).
Legitimate helpdesk or identity-management tooling enumerating accounts.
Domain-joined servers resolving group membership (machine accounts, excluded).
query: event.code:"5145" and winlog.event_data.RelativeTargetName:"samr" and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("Nessus" or "manageengine" or "svc_nessus" or "scanuser") and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$

name: Windows — Remote Service Execution via SMB Named Pipe (PsExec / Impacket)
description: Detects remote access to the Service Control Manager (svcctl), the PsExec service pipe (PSEXESVC) or the Task Scheduler ATSVC pipe over SMB. This is the core mechanism behind PsExec, Impacket smbexec/atexec/psexec and most hands-on-keyboard lateral movement. Detection is based on Windows Security event 5145 (detailed file share access), so it works on every host that audits share access and does NOT require Sysmon or command-line auditing — both of which are only partially deployed at JCB. Known vulnerability-scanner and monitoring service accounts, and machine accounts, are excluded.
author: ScanWave
note:
### Triage
1. Identify the **source** of the SMB session: correlate `winlog.event_data.SubjectLogonId` with event 4624 on the same host to recover `source.ip` and the logon type (expect Type 3 / Network).
2. Check the destination host for a **new service** immediately afterwards: events 7045 (System channel) and 4697 (Security channel).
3. Look for a matching binary drop on `C$`/`ADMIN$` — see the companion rule *Windows — Executable or Script Written to an Administrative Share*.
4. `PSEXESVC` or `svcctl` from a **user** account (not a machine account, not Nessus/ManageEngine) toward a server is treated as confirmed interactive lateral movement until proven otherwise.

### Tuning
Add legitimate admin jump hosts or deployment service accounts to an exception list rather than widening the query.
false_positives: Authenticated vulnerability scans (Nessus) and ManageEngine agent deployment — already excluded by account name.
SCCM/Intune or other software-deployment tooling that installs services remotely.
IT administrators using Sysinternals PsExec for legitimate remote support.
query: event.code:"5145" and winlog.event_data.RelativeTargetName:("svcctl" or "PSEXESVC" or "atsvc") and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:("Nessus" or "manageengine" or "svc_nessus" or "scanuser") and not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$

name: Windows Sandbox with Sensitive Configuration [NBI-4688]

Windows Sandbox is a lightweight virtual environment designed to safely run untrusted applications. It isolates processes from the host system, preventing permanent changes. However, adversaries can exploit this by configuring the sandbox to access host resources, enabling network connections, or executing commands at startup. The detection rule identifies such misuse by monitoring specific process activities and configurations indicative of potential abuse, such as unauthorized file system access or network enablement, helping analysts spot and mitigate threats effectively.

### Possible investigation steps

process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and

name: Windows — Scheduled Task Created with Suspicious Action
description:
Attacker objective
Create a scheduled task that runs attacker code for persistence or delayed/repeated execution.

Attack logic
Attackers register tasks that launch obfuscated PowerShell, scripting hosts, download cradles or binaries from user-writable paths, so the payload runs on a trigger or schedule.

Why this detection works
Scheduled-task-creation auditing (4698) records the full task definition; matching suspicious action/command patterns in the task content isolates malicious tasks, independent of case.

False positives
A legitimate administrative or software task that happens to invoke PowerShell with these arguments.

Tuning
Allowlist verified task authors/names; treat encoded/hidden/download tasks as high-risk.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4698 (TaskName, TaskContent).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Read the task action/command and the author (SubjectUserName).
2. If the action is an encoded/hidden/download command, remove the task and investigate the author and host.
false_positives: A legitimate administrative or software task that happens to invoke PowerShell with these arguments.
query:
FROM logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE event.code == "4698" AND winlog.event_data.TaskContent IS NOT NULL
| EVAL tc = TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.TaskContent)
| WHERE (tc LIKE "*powershell*" AND (tc LIKE "*-enc*" OR tc LIKE "*frombase64*" OR tc LIKE "*downloadstring*" OR tc LIKE "*downloadfile*" OR tc LIKE "*invoke-expression*" OR tc LIKE "*webclient*" OR tc LIKE "*iex(*" OR tc LIKE "*iex *"))
   OR tc LIKE "*mshta*"
   OR (tc LIKE "*regsvr32*" AND tc LIKE "*scrobj*")
   OR (tc LIKE "*rundll32*" AND (tc LIKE "*javascript*" OR tc LIKE "*comsvcs*"))
   OR (tc LIKE "*certutil*" AND tc LIKE "*urlcache*")
   OR (tc LIKE "*bitsadmin*" AND tc LIKE "*transfer*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, winlog.event_data.TaskName, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName, winlog.event_data.TaskContent

name: Defense Evasion / Lateral Movement — Service Account Interactive Logon (Type 2/10)
description: A service/privileged-named account logged on interactively (console Type 2 or RDP Type 10). Service accounts should authenticate via network (Type 3) only; interactive use indicates hands-on-keyboard misuse of a stolen service credential.
note:
### Investigation
1. Which host and source.ip? Is this account expected to be used interactively?
2. Review subsequent activity from that session.
### Tuning
If an admin legitimately uses a *.admin account interactively on a PAW, allowlist that account+host pair after validation.
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Break-glass/admin accounts used interactively on privileged access workstations (validate + allowlist account+host).
query: event.code:"4624" and (winlog.event_data.LogonType:"2" or winlog.event_data.LogonType:"10") and winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:(*sys_user or *.servacc or *.prod or ICBS* or SIGCAP* or Forti.* or custody* or CITRIX* or Docsafe or WSS.User or SP.admin or named* or PAM or igrafxsso* or FileNet* or Office365 or Internal.services or InnScanService or TeamMatese or Solarwinds* or Veeam* or Vynamic*)

name: Windows — Service Installed from a Suspicious Path
description: Detects a new Windows service whose binary path (ServiceFileName) resides in a user-writable or temporary directory (Temp, AppData, ProgramData, Public, PerfLogs). Legitimate services run from Program Files or System32; user-writable paths indicate persistence or lateral-movement tooling.
note:
## Investigation
1. `SubjectUserName` installed service `ServiceName` with binary `ServiceFileName` on `host.name`.
2. Inspect the binary; check whether it was created recently and by whom.
## Response
Stop/remove the service, quarantine the binary, and investigate the installing account.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.code:"4697" and winlog.event_data.ServiceFileName:(*\\Temp\\* or *\\AppData\\* or *\\ProgramData\\* or *\\Users\\Public\\* or *\\Windows\\Temp\\* or *\\PerfLogs\\*)

name: Windows — Service Installed with Suspicious Image Path
description:
Attacker objective
Install a new Windows service whose image is a command interpreter, script, or a binary in a user-writable path — for persistence or remote code execution.

Attack logic
Legitimate services run vendor executables from Program Files/System32. A service configured to launch cmd/powershell, a scripting host, an encoded command, or a binary under Temp/AppData is a persistence or lateral-execution mechanism (also used by PsExec-style tools).

Why this detection works
Service-installation auditing (4697) records the service image path; matching interpreter/encoded/user-writable-path patterns isolates malicious services, independent of case.

False positives
A poorly packaged legitimate service that runs a script (rare in a managed estate).

Tuning
Allowlist verified service names/paths; correlate with the installing account and source host.

Required telemetry
Windows Security 4697 (ServiceName, ServiceFileName).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Review the service name, image path and installing account.
2. A shell/encoded/temp-path service is persistence or remote execution — isolate and remove if unauthorised.
3. Correlate with a network logon (PsExec-style lateral) or preceding compromise.
false_positives: A poorly packaged legitimate service that runs a script (rare in a managed estate).
query:
FROM logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE event.code == "4697" AND winlog.event_data.ServiceFileName IS NOT NULL
| EVAL svc = TO_LOWER(winlog.event_data.ServiceFileName)
| WHERE svc LIKE "*cmd.exe*" OR svc LIKE "*powershell*" OR svc LIKE "*pwsh*" OR svc LIKE "*rundll32*" OR svc LIKE "*regsvr32*" OR svc LIKE "*mshta*" OR svc LIKE "*cscript*" OR svc LIKE "*wscript*" OR svc LIKE "*windows*temp*" OR svc LIKE "*appdata*" OR svc LIKE "*-enc*" OR svc LIKE "*frombase64*" OR svc LIKE "*downloadstring*" OR svc LIKE "*comspec*"
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, winlog.event_data.ServiceName, winlog.event_data.ServiceFileName, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Creation of Shadow Copy with wmic and powershell
description: Detects shadow copy creation for backup evasion
query: process.name : ("wmic.exe" OR "powershell.exe")  AND process.args : *shadowcopy*

name: Windows — Signed Binary Proxy Execution (LOLBin)
description:
Attacker objective
Execute attacker code through a trusted, signed Windows binary to bypass application control and evade defenses.

Attack logic
regsvr32 (scrobj/COM scriptlets), rundll32/mshta (inline javascript/vbscript), InstallUtil and MSBuild can run attacker-supplied code while appearing as trusted system binaries.

Why this detection works
Process command-line auditing records the proxy-execution argument patterns (scriptlet URLs, inline script protocols, uninstall-method abuse), independent of case.

False positives
Rare legitimate use of these binaries with scriptlet/inline-script arguments.

Tuning
Allowlist verified administrative scripts; review the referenced scriptlet/URL.

Required telemetry
Process creation with command line: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. Inspect the scriptlet/URL or inline script the binary was told to execute.
2. If malicious, isolate the host and hunt for the follow-on payload and parent process.
false_positives: Rare legitimate use of these binaries with scriptlet/inline-script arguments.
query:
FROM logs-windows.sysmon_operational-*,logs-system.security-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE (event.code == "1" OR event.code == "4688") AND process.command_line IS NOT NULL
| EVAL cl = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE (cl LIKE "*regsvr32*" AND (cl LIKE "*scrobj*" OR cl LIKE "*/i:http*" OR cl LIKE "*-i:http*" OR cl LIKE "*.sct*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*rundll32*" AND (cl LIKE "*javascript:*" OR cl LIKE "*vbscript:*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*mshta*" AND (cl LIKE "*javascript:*" OR cl LIKE "*vbscript:*"))
   OR (cl LIKE "*installutil*" AND cl LIKE "*/logfile=*" AND cl LIKE "*/u*")
   OR (cl LIKE "*msbuild*" AND cl LIKE "*http*")
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, process.command_line, event.code, winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName

name: Windows — Single Account Failing From Many Sources
description: One user account failed network sign-in (Windows 4625, logon type 3) from 5 or more DISTINCT source IPs within an hour — a distributed credential attack (password guessing / credential stuffing) against a single account, the many-sources-to-one-user pattern that the single-source spray primary does not cover. NBI baseline: normal users fail from <=4 distinct sources over a WEEK (typically their own workstation, laptop, Citrix and phone) and <=2 in any hour; only the SRLCL service account legitimately fails from many sources (a stuck/rotating password deployed on ~22 hosts, running processes via 4688) and is excluded as an evidence-backed known service account. Machine accounts (*$) are excluded from THIS analytic because their observed many-source failures are benign auto-managed-credential retry, and machine-account credential abuse is covered by separate account/host-compromise analytics. Keyed on distinct-SOURCE cardinality per account in a short window, so a legitimate multi-device user does not trip it but a coordinated attack against one identity does.
note:
### Investigation — one account attacked from many sources
1. **WHO / TO WHAT** `winlog.event_data.TargetUserName` — the account under attack. Is it a normal human user (should fail from <=4 sources/week) or a shared/service account?
2. **DID WHAT / FROM WHERE** it failed network sign-in from >=5 distinct source IPs in an hour. Pull those source IPs (4625 for this account) — internal workstations, a NAT/proxy egress, or unrelated/external hosts (distributed attack)?
3. **WHY suspicious** breadth of ORIGINS against one identity = distributed guessing/stuffing; correlate `winlog.event_data.SubStatus` (0xc000006a bad-password from many sources).
4. **Escalate** if the account then SUCCEEDS from any of those sources (see the brute-force-success companion) — treat as compromise; force a reset. De-escalate only after confirming a new legitimate shared/service account (add to known_infrastructure service accounts by evidence, not a blanket allowlist).

standard.rule_type_rationale: D0 observable = cardinality of distinct SOURCE IPs per target account crossing a baselined number; D2 (cardinality IS the behavior) -> Threshold with cardinality (key = TargetUserName, cardinality = source.ip). Companion to the source->many-users primary; different key covers the many-sources->one-user evasion.
standard.baseline: normal users <=4 distinct sources/7d, <=2/24h; threshold 5/1h; SRLCL (service, 22 sources/1h) excluded

exclusion_record.evidence: SRLCL runs processes (4688), 7/7 days, peak 22 sources/1h = stuck-password service; machine accounts auto-managed high-entropy
exclusion_record.fp_reduction: removes the only current high-cardinality account
exclusion_record.coverage_lost: a distributed attack specifically against SRLCL
exclusion_record.evasion_introduced: attacker targets SRLCL (a service account) — compensated by the fail->success correlation

standard.replaces: raad-13-per-user-distributed-spray (noisy cross-surface: o365 empty, FortiGate user null; fired on SRLCL + multi-device users)

query: event.code:"4625" and winlog.event_data.LogonType:"3" and source.ip:* and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:"ANONYMOUS LOGON" and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:*$ and not winlog.event_data.TargetUserName:"SRLCL"

name: Windows — UAC Bypass via Auto-Elevated LOLBin
description:
Attacker objective
Elevate from a medium-integrity to a high-integrity process without a consent prompt by abusing a Windows auto-elevating binary (UAC bypass).

Attack logic
Several trusted Windows binaries auto-elevate and can be hijacked (via registry/COM manipulation) to launch an attacker process elevated. The tell is an auto-elevating binary spawning a command interpreter or scripting host.

Why this detection works
Process-creation lineage links the auto-elevating parent to a shell/scripting child on the same event, a combination that does not occur in normal use.

False positives
Rare legitimate automation that launches a shell from one of these binaries.

Tuning
Allowlist verified parent/child pairs if a legitimate workflow triggers it.

Required telemetry
Process creation with parent process: Sysmon Event ID 1 and Windows Security 4688 (process.parent.name).
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. The parent (auto-elevated binary) launched a shell/scripting child — a UAC-bypass pattern.
2. Review the child command line for the follow-on action; investigate the user and host.

false_positives: Rare legitimate automation that launches a shell from one of these binaries.

1. `SubjectUserName` on `host.name` ran `process.command_line`.

  not (process.name == "code-tunnel.exe" and process.args == "status" and process.parent.name == "Code.exe")

name: Suspicious Execution from a WebDav Share [NBI-4688]
tags: Data Source: Windows Security Event Logs
Data Source: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
description: Identifies attempt to execute Windows scripts from a remote WebDav Share. Adversaries may abuse this method to evade dropping malicious files to victim file system.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

### Investigating Suspicious Execution from a WebDav Share

#### Possible investigation steps

- Check if the remote webdav server is autorized by the organization.
- Check all the downloaded files from the remote server and their content.
- Investigate the process execution chain (parent process tree) to identify the initial vector.
- Investigate other alerts associated with the user/host during the past 5 minutes.
- Identify the user account that performed the action and whether it should perform this kind of action.
- Identify the target computer and its role in the IT environment.
- Investigate what commands were run, and assess whether this behavior is prevalent in the environment by looking for similar occurrences across hosts.

### Response and remediation

- Initiate the incident response process based on the outcome of the triage.
- Isolate the involved hosts to prevent further post-compromise behavior.
- Investigate credential exposure on systems compromised or used by the attacker to ensure all compromised accounts are identified. Reset passwords for these accounts and other potentially compromised credentials, such as email, business systems, and
author: raadabujaish
false_positives: Trusted webdav shares used to host trusted content.
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
 process.name : ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "conhost.exe", "wscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "msiexec.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "net.exe") and
 process.command_line : ("*trycloudflare.com*", "*@SSL\\*", "*\\webdav\\*", "*\\DavWWWRoot\\*", "*\\\\*.*@8080\\*", "*\\\\*.*@80\\*", "*\\\\*.*@8443\\*", "*\\\\*.*@443\\*") and
 not (process.name : "cmd.exe" and process.args : "\\\\?\\UNC\\*.sharepoint.com@SSL\\DavWWWRoot\\*")

name: Windows — Windows Account or Group Discovery
description: This rule identifies the execution of commands that enumerates account or group information. Adversaries may use built-in applications to get a listing of local system or domain accounts and groups.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and
(
  (
   (
    (process.name : "net.exe" or process.pe.original_file_name == "net.exe") or
    (
     (process.name : "net1.exe" or process.pe.original_file_name == "net1.exe") and
     not process.parent.name : "net.exe"
    )
   ) and process.args : ("accounts", "group", "user", "localgroup") and not process.args : "/add"
  ) or
  (process.name:("dsquery.exe", "dsget.exe") and process.args:("*members*", "user")) or
  (process.name:"dsquery.exe" and process.args:"*filter*") or
  process.name:("quser.exe", "qwinsta.exe", "PsGetSID.exe", "PsLoggedOn.exe", "LogonSessions.exe", "whoami.exe") or
  (
    process.name: "cmd.exe" and
    (
      process.args : "echo" and process.args : (
        "%username%", "%userdomain%", "%userdnsdomain%",
        "%userdomain_roamingprofile%", "%userprofile%",
        "%homepath%", "%localappdata%", "%appdata%"
      ) or
      process.args : "set"
    )
  )
) and not process.parent.args: "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\\Content\\DetectionScripts\\*.ps1"
and not process.parent.name : "LTSVC.exe" and not user.id : "S-1-5-18"

name: Windows — Windows System Network Connections Discovery
description: This rule identifies the execution of commands that can be used to enumerate network connections. Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from a compromised system to identify targets within an environment.
author: raadabujaish
query:
process where event.type == "start" and
(
  process.name : "netstat.exe" or
  (
   (
    (process.name : "net.exe" or process.pe.original_file_name == "net.exe") or
    (
     (process.name : "net1.exe" or process.pe.original_file_name == "net1.exe") and
     not process.parent.name : "net.exe"
    )
   ) and process.args : ("use", "user", "session", "config") and not process.args: ("/persistent:*", "/delete", "\\\\*")
  ) or
  (process.name : "nbtstat.exe" and process.args : "-s*")
) and not user.id : "S-1-5-18"

name: WMI Incoming Lateral Movement [NBI-4688]
description: Identifies processes executed via Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) on a remote host. This could be indicative of adversary lateral movement, but could be noisy if administrators use WMI to remotely manage hosts.
note:
## Coverage
This rule runs on Windows Security 4688 process-creation events. Command-line-dependent conditions currently apply to hosts where command-line auditing is enabled.

## Detection guidance
## Triage and analysis

> **Disclaimer**:
> This investigation guide was created using generative AI technology and has been reviewed to improve its accuracy and relevance. While every effort has been made to ensure its quality, we recommend validating the content and adapting it to suit your specific environment and operational needs.

### Investigating WMI Incoming Lateral Movement

Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is a core Windows feature enabling remote management and data collection. Adversaries exploit WMI for lateral movement by executing processes on remote hosts, often bypassing traditional security measures. The detection rule identifies suspicious WMI activity by monitoring specific network connections and process executions, filtering out common false positives to highlight potential threats.

### Possible investigation steps

- Review the source IP address of the incoming RPC connection to determine if it is from a known or trusted network segment, excluding localhost addresses like 127.0.0.1 and ::1.
- Check the process name and parent process name, specifically looking for svchost.exe and WmiPrvSE.exe, to confirm the execution context and identify any unusua
author: raadabujaish
query:
sequence by host.id with maxspan = 20s

 /* Accepted Incoming RPC connection by Winmgmt service */

  [network where host.os.type == "windows" and process.name : "svchost.exe" and network.direction : ("incoming", "ingress") and
   source.ip != "127.0.0.1" and source.ip != "::1" and destination.port == 135]

  /* Excluding Common FPs Nessus and SCCM */

  [process where host.os.type == "windows" and event.type == "start" and process.parent.name : "WmiPrvSE.exe" and
   not (?process.Ext.token.integrity_level_name : "System" or ?winlog.event_data.IntegrityLevel : "System") and
   not (
         user.id : ("S-1-5-18", "S-1-5-19", "S-1-5-20") and
         /* Don't apply the user.id exclusion to Sysmon for compatibility */
         not event.dataset : ("windows.sysmon_operational", "windows.sysmon")
   ) and
   not process.executable :
               ("?:\\Program Files\\HPWBEM\\Tools\\hpsum_swdiscovery.exe",
                "?:\\Windows\\CCM\\Ccm32BitLauncher.exe",
                "?:\\Windows\\System32\\wbem\\mofcomp.exe",
                "?:\\Windows\\Microsoft.NET\\Framework*\\csc.exe",
                "?:\\Windows\\System32\\powercfg.exe") and
   not (process.executable : "?:\\Windows\\System32\\msiexec.exe" and process.args : "REBOOT=ReallySuppress") and
   not (process.executable : "?:\\Windows\\System32\\inetsrv\\appcmd.exe" and process.args : "uninstall")
   ]

name: FIM — Monitored System Executable/Driver Deleted
description: Detects deletion of a monitored executable, DLL or driver on a protected server. Deletion of system binaries can indicate defence tooling being removed, malware self-cleanup, or destructive activity.
note:
## Investigation
1. `file.path` is the removed binary; determine whether it was a security/monitoring component.
2. Correlate with process activity on the host.
## Response
If a security component was removed, isolate and investigate.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:"deleted" and file.extension:("exe" or "dll" or "sys")

name: FIM — New Executable or DLL Created in a Windows System Directory
description: Detects a NEW executable, DLL or driver file appearing in a protected Windows system directory (System32/SysWOW64/drivers) on a monitored server. Legitimate binaries there change during patching (attributes_modified/updated); a brand-new binary is a strong indicator of malware drop, DLL side-loading, or a malicious driver.
note:
## Investigation
1. `file.path`/`file.name` is the new binary; `file.hash.sha256/sha1` — pivot to threat intel; `file.owner` and `host.name` give context.
2. Correlate with Windows 4688/PowerShell and Kaspersky on the same host/time.
## Response
If unknown/unsigned, quarantine the file and investigate the host for compromise.
author: raadabujaish
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:"created" and file.extension:("exe" or "dll" or "sys") and file.path:(*System32* or *SysWOW64* or *\\drivers\\*)

name: Host — Mass File Change Burst (Possible Ransomware or Destruction)
description:
Attacker objective
Encrypt, overwrite or destroy files at scale — ransomware or a wiper rapidly writing, renaming and deleting many files on a host.

Attack logic
Ransomware and destructive malware touch a large number of files in a short window (encrypt-in-place, rename to a new extension, or delete). A host generating an unusually high volume of distinct file changes is exhibiting this pattern.

Why this detection works
Aggregating distinct changed files per host over the file-integrity stream distinguishes a mass-change burst from the routine handful of file changes a host makes during normal operation and patching.

False positives
A large software deployment, OS upgrade, or bulk migration/backup job on the host.

Tuning
Set the per-host file-count threshold above the routine change rate; allowlist scheduled deployment/patch windows and hosts; note that coverage is limited to FIM-monitored paths, so user-data encryption outside those paths may not be visible.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): event.action, file.path, file.extension, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. host.name is the affected host; review the volume of creates/renames/deletes and the file extensions.
2. A burst of renames to a common new extension, or mass deletion, indicates ransomware/wiper — isolate the host immediately.
3. Correlate with Kaspersky/Defender detections and the host's backup status; confirm against any planned deployment.
false_positives: A large software deployment, OS upgrade, or bulk migration/backup job on the host.
query:
FROM logs-fim.event-* METADATA _id, _index, _version
| WHERE event.dataset == "fim.event" AND event.action IN ("created","updated","moved","deleted") AND host.name IS NOT NULL
| STATS files = COUNT_DISTINCT(file.path), creates = COUNT(CASE(event.action=="created",1,null)), renames = COUNT(CASE(event.action=="moved",1,null)), deletes = COUNT(CASE(event.action=="deleted",1,null)), extensions = VALUES(file.extension) BY host.name
| WHERE files >= 100

name: Windows — Kernel Driver (.sys) Created in a System Directory
description:
Attacker objective
Load malicious kernel code or a vulnerable driver (bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver) to gain kernel-level control, disable security tooling, or hide activity (rootkit).

Attack logic
Kernel drivers (.sys) placed in the system drivers directory can execute in kernel mode. Attackers drop a malicious or known-vulnerable driver there as a precursor to loading it. New driver files in this location are rare and high-risk.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records the creation of .sys files in the drivers directory, surfacing driver drops at the filesystem level even without process context.

False positives
Legitimate driver installation via Windows Update, an OEM/hardware driver package, or a software installer.

Tuning
Allowlist verified driver-deployment/patch processes; correlate with driver-load events and signature status; prioritise unsigned or unexpected driver names.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path (drivers directory), file.extension, event.action, file.hash, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.name/file.hash identify the driver and host.name the system; check the hash reputation and signature.
2. Confirm whether the driver came from a legitimate update/installer; an unknown or unsigned driver is high-risk (BYOVD/rootkit).
3. Correlate the hash with Kaspersky/Defender and hunt for the driver being loaded.
false_positives: Legitimate driver installation via Windows Update, an OEM/hardware driver package, or a software installer.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:"created" and file.extension:("sys" or "SYS") and file.path:*drivers*

name: Windows — Scheduled Task Definition File Created or Modified
description:
Attacker objective
Persist or execute code on a schedule by creating or modifying a Windows scheduled task, whose definition is stored as a file under the system Tasks directory.

Attack logic
Windows stores each scheduled task as an XML definition file under the system Tasks folder. Creating or altering one of these files corresponds to creating or changing a scheduled task — a common persistence and execution technique.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records writes to the Tasks directory, surfacing scheduled-task changes at the filesystem level even where task-scheduler event logging is unavailable.

False positives
Legitimate software installation/update, Group Policy, or administration that creates scheduled tasks.

Tuning
Allowlist known software-deployment and management tooling; correlate with Windows scheduled-task events (4698) and the task's action/command where available; prioritise servers.

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path (system Tasks directory), event.action, host.name.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.path names the task definition and host.name the system.
2. Correlate with Windows event 4698 (scheduled task created) to identify the task action and the creating account (not captured by FIM).
3. Review the task's command/trigger; an unexpected task is persistence — remove and investigate.
false_positives: Legitimate software installation/update, Group Policy, or administration that creates scheduled tasks.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:("created" or "updated") and file.path:*\\System32\\Tasks\\*
